Pakistani astronaut to join Chinese space mission

November 24, 2026

A Pakistani astronaut is set to become to the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a payload specialist, will join the Shenzhou-24 mission when it launches on Wednesday.

China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission launches from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT) on Wednesday.

"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.

"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.

Pakistan: 'Source of joy and pride'

Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.

"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," said Ali.

"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit."

What will Pakistani astronaut Ali do in space?

Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.

During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.

China has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.

Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant step in relations between Islamabad and Beijing.

Rivalling the US

Pakistan, which maintains close diplomatic and trade ties with Beijing, is a natural partner in the endeavour.

Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.

Tang told reporters that learning to work together was more challenging in this mission, pointing to differences in language, culture and even psychology. But efforts from both sides have been paying off, Tang said.

“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language," he said, adding that he and Wu also stepped up their English learning.

The Long March-2F rocket that will carry the crew into space will soon be filled with propellant, the CMSA's Zhang said.

Why it is here: original reporting, corporate governance

Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO may have eased concerns over the chipmaker's leadership, but it has also brought renewed scrutiny to the company's corporate governance and its reliance on its founder.

Huang's abrupt departure and unexpected reinstatement exposed a deeper vulnerability at the heart of Nvidia, industry experts told CNBC, raising questions about board oversight and succession planning.

"What does it mean if you have a company too big to fail or a CEO too big to fire?" Angela Mancini, head of advisory for global risk insights at Dow Jones, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Tuesday.

Mancini pointed to Huang's unusually large number of direct reports as another sign of how heavily Nvidia depends on its founder.

"What does it mean when someone has 60 direct reports, and you literally are in a situation where you feel like you can't fire them?" she added.

For Nvidia, Huang's return offers an opportunity to address some of the governance issues brought to light by his departure.

An opportunity for change

Jeff Herbst, managing partner at GFT Ventures and a former Nvidia executive who spent nearly two decades at the company, said he had written to the board late last week calling for Huang's return.

While initially disappointed by the allegations surrounding Huang, Herbst said he came to view the episode as an opportunity for Nvidia to strengthen its governance, succession planning and overall management.

"While a lot of people saw a crisis here, I saw a potential opportunity," he said.

Herbst said Nvidia's management and oversight functions needed to evolve alongside its transformation from a relatively small technology company into one of the world's largest corporations.

"I think the corporate governance, the succession planning, the legal function, the regulatory function, the political function, all has to scale at the same time," he said.

He suggested Nvidia add more experience to its board by bringing in individuals who have run large companies and take a more formal approach to developing potential successors to Huang.

Tom Hulick, CEO of Strategy Asset Managers, agreed, saying the chip giant's "corporate governance definitely needs to be retooled."

It's "unheard of" and "unprecedented" for a president to enforce the reinstatement of a company's CEO, Hulick said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.

"He's a born leader. He's enduring a lot of pain right now. Does he deserve to be back as CEO? It's not for me to speculate. Is he the right person? Probably for now."

However, Hulick added that the company still has "a lot of things to worry about" regarding corporate governance.

The succession question

Huang's departure also exposed how closely Nvidia's leadership and long-term strategy are tied to its founder, raising questions about how the company would navigate a future transition.

Stacy Rasgon, managing director and senior U.S. semiconductor analyst at Bernstein Research, said the episode had revived attention to a risk investors had long overlooked.

"We all knew that there was key man risk here. We all chose, and I'm including myself in that. We all kind of chose to just ignore it," Rasgon told CNBC.

Succession planning, he said, is an issue both Huang and the board will need to address and communicate clearly to investors.

"I think both Jensen and the board will have to figure out, and I think communicate to investors," he added.

Herbst also pointed to Huang's personal role in driving Nvidia's technological innovations, including his willingness to invest in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing long before those businesses became profitable.

New markets such as autonomous systems and robotics would require major investment and a leader with Huang's passion and vision, Herbst added.

item.title: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, space technology

What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

November 24, 2026

Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

What does history teach us?

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

How does the physics change in space?

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

Which systems would be exposed?

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

Is it legal, and could it be detected?

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Can the US protect itself?

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Could radioactive fallout reach the ground?

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed

Public outcry led to a legal battle when details surfaced of the plans to conduct two controlled detonations.

The United States military will proceed with its plan to blow up a deteriorating stockpile of toxic lead explosives in rural Iowa, according to the army’s top civilian official, after a federal appeals court gave clearance to the waste disposal operation.

In an announcement late Monday on X, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle called the choice to move forward a “consensus decision” among all the federal agencies involved, as well as the courts and state officials.

“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming governors say the call belongs to the experts,” Telle said.

“We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities.”

The Army prompted a public outcry last week when details surfaced of its plan to conduct two controlled detonations of 68 drums containing almost 4,500kg (10,000lb) of degraded lead azide, a chemical used in munitions, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.

Legal battle

Environmental groups immediately filed suit to block the plan, raising public safety concerns over the likelihood that the explosions would release a plume of toxic lead dust over homes, crops and livestock far beyond the detonation site, about 240km (150 miles) southeast of Des Moines.

The lawsuit challenged a special permit granted for the operation by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The EPA countered that a managed detonation would be far less risky than an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion of the highly volatile material, a scenario the agency said was growing more likely as the weather turns colder in Iowa.

According to the EPA, any attempt to chemically neutralise or relocate the storage drums would also risk an uncontrolled blast.

A three-judge panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals last Thursday issued a temporary stay blocking the EPA’s permit while the court more thoroughly reviewed the case.

But Trump administration lawyers filed a legal notice two days later asserting that the Army intended to carry out the controlled detonation with or without court approval, citing an emergency exemption to federal environmental laws.

Then, in another twist on Monday, US President Donald Trump weighed in on the controversy, ordering the Army to hold off on its disposal plan until the appeals court had ruled in its favour.

Hours after Trump’s edict on Monday pausing the army’s demolition plan, the 8th Circuit sided with the EPA and lifted the court’s earlier stay, removing the final legal obstacle. But the status of the detonation plan remained unclear until Telle’s announcement on Monday night.

item.title: Oldest known quasar formed 630 million years after the big bang
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail

Only four months after setting its own record, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid space telescope has outdone itself yet again. In a study published today in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics, ESA researchers announce the discovery of the most distant—and therefore oldest—quasar ever observed. The object now classified as J1504+6252 formed just 630 million years after the big bang, making it 40 million years older than the quasar Euclid spotted in July. Euclid’s new image is equivalent to viewing J1504+6252 as it existed about 13.1 billion years ago, when the universe was only five percent its current age.

A quasar is the result of a galactic core’s supermassive black hole inhaling cosmic gas and dust while simultaneously spewing tremendous amounts of energy. During this comparatively brief phase in a galaxy’s lifecycle, the nucleus can actually shine brighter than the entire system itself. But even such a luminous object like quasar J1504+6252 can be hard to spot when it is located deep within space-time.

However, Euclid excels at finding these and other elusive objects. The ESA launched its space telescope in 2023 to examine the mysterious realm of dark matter and dark energy. Despite estimates that these forces account for about 95 percent of the universe, astronomers still know very little about them. Identifying subjects like quasars allows researchers invaluable opportunities to learn more about dark matter and dark energy, as well as their roles in the early, formative eons of the cosmos.

J1504+6252 is so young and gargantuan that it’s confounding astronomers. Based on their initial assessments, it’s unclear how a quasar with a mass equivalent to about 360 million suns even formed so early in cosmic history.

It also has the largest redshift on record. Redshifting occurs when light waves stretch towards the infrared spectrum as they travel through the universe. The greater the redshift, the older its source is. In barely 1.5 years, Euclid has flagged 31 quasars, including 12 beyond a redshift of 7.

J1504+6252 is the first quasar to possess a redshift beyond 8. Despite its age, J1504+6252 is devouring material at a comparatively slow pace. This implies it attained its size during unprecedentedly fast growth spurts early in its life—a feature that challenges existing models of black hole formation.

Astronomers have nicknamed the quasar Dún Aonghasa to honor its age and location. The actual Dún Aonghasa is a prehistoric clifftop fort in Ireland overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Like the ancient structure itself, J1504+6252 is situated at the edge of the visible cosmos. That said, astronomers expect Euclid to find multiple more quasars beyond redshift 8 in the years to come.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence, and concrete detail

New quasar record tightens constraints on black hole formation scenarios

A team of astronomers led by Julien Wolf, a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany (now at the European Southern Observatory in Garching bei München, Germany), discovered the most distant quasar to date. First identified in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the object was confirmed to be a quasar by subsequent observations with some of the most powerful telescopes on the ground and in space.

After the W. M. Keck Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope provided the first hints, the Large Binocular Telescope and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope revealed a redshift of z = 8.13, corresponding to a cosmic age of 630 million years after the Big Bang.

Redshift is a measure of how much the wavelength of the light emitted at the source has been stretched due to cosmic expansion by the time it reaches the telescope. Depending on how the cosmos evolved over time, this redshift can be translated into a distance. Commonly referred to as J1504+6252 and nicknamed "Dún Aonghasa" by the team, this quasar existed 40 million years earlier than the previous record holder and is the first quasar with a redshift greater than eight.

The findings are published in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The brightest lasting objects in the universe

Quasars are intensely bright galaxy cores with supermassive black holes caught in the act of feeding: Material in their immediate vicinity forms a turbulent swirl of gas that heats until it glows brighter than an entire galaxy before it falls into the black hole. Astronomers call this kind of process accretion. Quasars are the most luminous persistent sources in the universe, which is why they can be studied in detail even within the first billion years of cosmic history. Follow-up observations revealed that Dún Aonghasa harbors a supermassive black hole with a mass several hundred million times that of the sun.

Looking for quasars at the earliest epochs of the universe by pushing current observational capabilities to the extreme isn't simply a hunt for new records, though. "Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centers grew," says Wolf. "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth—or both." This puts strict constraints on the mechanisms that helped increase their masses so vastly and quickly.

Scenarios of black hole formation

Wolf and his colleagues calculated the conditions under which the proposed scenarios could produce black holes as massive as the one powering the quasar Dún Aonghasa. Considering reasonable growth rates, the latest discoveries seem to be consistent with a direct collapse scenario, in which a massive gas cloud condenses under its own gravity and directly forms a black hole that subsequently continues to grow. The growth rate is usually constrained by the Eddington limit, set by a self-regulating mechanism that repels the collapsing gas at increasingly high temperatures.

Interestingly, observational data indicate that Dún Aonghasa is growing far below that limit, which shows that even the most distant quasars collect gas at varying rates. If this quasar had always grown this slowly, it would have required an extremely massive initial seed, which is difficult to explain with current formation models. Instead, an early black hole as massive as the one in Dún Aonghasa supports the idea of much more rapid accretion in the past, perhaps even beyond the theoretical Eddington limit.

Altogether, the conditions for a direct collapse to happen must have been rare during this era of cosmic evolution, which could explain the few quasars found at redshifts beyond 7.5 so far. If, at some point, astronomers discover quasars at considerably higher redshifts, that is, approaching a cosmic age of just a few hundred million years, even the direct collapse scenario may become less likely.

In this case, astronomers may have to consider yet another, more exotic alternative: primordial black holes—hypothetical black holes formed right after the Big Bang that would function as massive seeds for gas to accumulate. Even without requiring extreme growth rates, such massive objects would provide a head start, giving the black holes ample time to gain millions upon millions of solar masses. Only future observations and discoveries of perhaps even more distant quasars will fully resolve the puzzle of how they formed.

This striking satellite snap shows a heavy blanket of snow surrounding a growing lava dome at the summit of one of Russia's most active and unstable volcanoes.

The snow-covered peak, called Shiveluch (also spelled Shivelyuch or Sheveluch), is a 10,771-foot-tall (3,283 meters) stratovolcano. The name Shiveluch loosely translates to "smoking mountain" in the language of the region's Indigenous Itelmen people. It is the northernmost active peak in the Kamchatka Peninsula, a highly volcanic region in eastern Russia that's famous for its unusually powerful and dramatically beautiful eruptions.

Shiveluch stands out even among its extremely active volcanic neighbors and is one of the planet's most active volcanoes, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. It has experienced at least 15 eruptions in the past 100 years, the most recent of which has been going on since 1999, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

On average, the volcano spews around 530 million cubic feet (15 million cubic meters) of lava every year — enough to fill 6,000 Olympic-size swimming pools, according to a 2007 study. As a result, its appearance constantly changes when viewed from above.

"On a near-daily basis, satellites detect new signs of activity within [Shiveluch's] horseshoe-shaped caldera, including thermal anomalies, hot avalanches and debris flows," Earth Observatory representatives wrote. The volcano is also constantly spitting out "ash deposits that darken the surrounding landscape," they added.

In this image, you might be able to see a particularly dark circle at the top of the volcano's caldera. This is a lava dome — a steep-sided landform that emerges when lava piles up on top of a volcanic vent — that has been growing rapidly in recent months, according to the Earth Observatory.

The lava within this swelling blob is "extruded slowly and piles up into lobed, sloped, or spine-like shapes akin to those that form when toothpaste is squeezed from a tube," Earth Observatory representatives wrote.

This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine.

Sandra Tiguila, an adventurous eater, enjoyed a bison sausage breakfast sandwich while dining out in August of 2025. On the drive home, she noticed a rash appearing on her wrist. The burning sensation spread to her arms and legs, making it nearly impossible to sleep. In the days to come, she tried creams, pills, injections; nothing helped.

Ten days later, Tiguila ate out again, ordering a steak. When her face swelled up, her boyfriend drove her to the emergency room. A doctor tested her for diseases carried by ticks. Tiguila, who lives in Carbondale, Illinois, had been bitten twice that June.

Tiguila went home and the next morning, as she was drinking coffee with her usual supplement of bovine collagen for joint, hair and nail health, the test results came in. She had developed a red meat allergy that’s activated by tick bites. “I immediately dumped that coffee down the sink,” says Tiguila. She started avoiding all mammal products — the main way to manage this rising and occasionally life-threatening allergy.

Known as alpha-gal syndrome, the condition arises when the immune system reacts to a certain sugar molecule, called alpha-gal, that’s found in red meat. Symptoms range from a mild rash or stomach upset to anaphylactic shock; in 2025, alpha-gal syndrome was blamed for the death of an otherwise healthy 47-year-old man. The syndrome has only recently been characterized and is still not fully understood. Though Tiguila, who is a nurse, was aware of the allergy, she says she still failed to connect her rash to her meaty meals and earlier tick bites.

As ticks have spread northward, so too have alpha-gal diagnoses. Up to 450,000 people in the United States may have been affected since 2010, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates.

“It’s emerging as one of the top adult-onset food allergies,” says Onyinye Iweala, an allergist and immunologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Odd, Even for an Allergy

Allergies are often mysterious, but this one is extra weird. “Alpha-gal follows none of the rules that I was taught in training about how a food allergy behaves,” says Maya Jerath, an allergist and immunologist at Washington University in St. Louis and one of Tiguila’s physicians. For example, unlike with other food allergies, where reactions are immediate, alpha-gal symptoms often show up hours after eating meat.

And, strangely, the allergy often arises after a tick bite. In the early 2000s, Jerath recalls, Australian allergist and clinician Sheryl van Nunen first shared tales on the scientific-conference circuit of patients with a delayed allergic reaction to red meat after tick bites. “Nobody believed her,” Jerath says.

The eventual unraveling of the mystery would happen on the other side of the world, where immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, unaware of van Nunen’s findings, was pursuing two parallel projects in his lab at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. In one, his group was collecting blood samples from people claiming weird meat sensitivities. In the other, they were investigating patients’ strange reactions to the cancer drug cetuximab. It would take both projects to crack the case, recalls Scott Commins, an allergist who was then part of the lab and now works at the University of North Carolina.

First, the cancer strand. Cetuximab is a drug designed to stick to cancer cells and block their overzealous growth. It was first approved to treat colorectal cancer in 2004, but as its testing and use spread, an odd pattern appeared. In the Southeastern United States, more than one in five patients had allergic reactions to the drug — hives, difficulty breathing and even anaphylaxis.

It took about a year and a half, Commins recalls, but Platts-Mills’ group found the culprit. People who reacted badly to cetuximab, they discovered, had blood loaded with proteins called IgE antibodies. When activated inappropriately, IgE causes allergies. The cancer patients with the allergic reactions to cetuximab had IgE antibodies that were reacting specifically to the sugar alpha-gal, the researchers reported in 2008.

Now, humans (and many other primates) don’t make alpha-gal. But most mammals do. It’s one of several sugars that cells attach to proteins to regulate their final structure and function. And cetuximab, like many drugs, is manufactured in lab-grown mouse cells. These cells had attached alpha-gal molecules to the cetuximab. That’s what triggered the allergic reactions in the cancer patients.

But it only happened in some of the people taking the drug. Why them? And why only in the Southeastern United States?

The next clues came from the lab’s other work, on meat sensitivities. This puzzle, of course, also involved exposure to tissues from non-primate mammals — so the researchers hypothesized that this allergy had the same cause as the drug reactions. Sure enough, they found that people with meat sensitivity also had elevated IgE antibodies to alpha-gal, causing a “novel and severe food allergy,” the team reported in 2009.

The allergy is bizarre for several reasons. There’s the delay that van Nunen had noticed. And food allergies are typically triggered by protein: egg protein, nut protein, etc. While some carbohydrates have been linked to mild allergies, a sugar causing such severe reactions was unheard of, says Jeffrey Wilson, an allergist and immunologist at UVA Health in Charlottesville, Virginia.

Plus, food allergies were supposed to be all-or-nothing: A person allergic to peanuts will always react to peanuts. Not so with alpha-gal. For example, some people react to meat alone; others might be bothered by dairy or other mammal products, such as gelatin in cosmetics or medications.…

Abstract

Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1–3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.

These strange geological features may offer clues to the Red Planet's watery past.

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

- Date:

- Summary:

Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of lifeâs earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering new clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the new evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious New Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection

At the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

"What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," said Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future."

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences

To uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

The databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

"The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically."

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions

Beyond identifying the new viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.…

Findings from the EVITA dengue trial conducted in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, showed 68.6% efficacy in reducing arboviral infections among participating children.

The results were presented at the American Society of Tropical Medicine & Hygiene annual meeting in National Harbor, Maryland.

The EVITA dengue (EValuate the efficacy of Wolbachia-InfecTed Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in reducing the incidence of Arboviral infection) trial is a four-year, school-based, cluster-randomized, controlled trial in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, led by an independent, multidisciplinary team of researchers from Brazil, including the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG), World Mosquito Program (WMP), Fiocruz and Faculdade de Medicina de São José do Rio Preto (FAMERP), and the United States—including Emory University, Yale University, Johns Hopkins University and the University of Florida.

The trial was designed to test whether releasing Aedes aegypti mosquitoes infected with Wolbachia (wMel strain) in school catchment areas could reduce arboviral infections in children living in those communities.

The study included 58 school-defined geographic clusters in Belo Horizonte, with 29 clusters assigned to receive releases of wMel mosquitoes in addition to standard vector-control measures and 29 clusters assigned to standard vector control alone (standard vector control consists of insecticidal sprays and mosquito source reduction).

Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium that, when transinfected into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, dramatically reduces the mosquito's ability to transmit several arboviruses such as dengue, Zika and chikungunya.

Once introduced into a mosquito population, Wolbachia is passed from female mosquitoes to their offspring, allowing it to spread through the local mosquito population and become stably established over time. The trial implemented releases of Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes from January 2021 through May 2022.

"We are pleased to have developed this locally adapted strain from Belo Horizonte for the EVITA dengue trial and to achieve successful sustained establishment of the Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes for over three years," says Luciano Moreira of Fiocruz and the World Mosquito Program in Brazil.

The EVITA trial was conducted in Brazil from 2020 to 2024 and enrolled 5,757 schoolchildren, ages 6 to 11. In 2024, Brazil experienced the largest recorded dengue outbreak in the country's history, contributing to the largest global dengue burden ever reported and providing an important setting to evaluate the intervention under conditions of intense transmission.

Participating children provided a baseline blood sample in 2020 and were followed with annual blood collections through 2024. Samples were tested for dengue, Zika and chikungunya antibodies.

"Conducting this study during the COVID-19 pandemic was an extraordinary challenge, particularly as schools closed just as we were beginning enrollment," says Mauro Teixeira, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) and co-principal investigator of the trial.

He added, "We are deeply grateful to the children, their families, the schools and the communities who supported this research. Their commitment, together with the dedication of the research team, made it possible to successfully follow this large cohort over several years and complete a study that has the potential to inform the future of arboviral disease prevention."

"Our findings in the EVITA trial show a 68.6% overall efficacy in reducing arboviral infection from this intervention," says Sri Edupuganti, co-principal investigator of the EVITA trial and professor in the Department of Medicine, Division of Infectious Diseases at Emory University School of Medicine. Specifically, for dengue, the efficacy was 68.5%, and for chikungunya, it was a bit higher at 73.3%.

"This means that children living in communities where Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were established had substantially lower arboviral infection."

These findings provide important evidence that the Wolbachia method could become a powerful new tool for preventing dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases.

The scale of the laboratory effort was substantial. Tens of thousands of blood samples were processed and tested in the laboratory of Mauricio Nogueira at FAMERP in São José do Rio Preto, Brazil.

"Processing and analyzing thousands of samples over several years required an enormous laboratory effort from our team. This rigorous work was essential to generating these results, which represent an important advance in the fight against arboviral diseases," says Nogueira.

"The EVITA trial findings represent an important step forward in the search for sustainable, scalable approaches to protect 4 billion of the world's population that live in regions, including parts of the U.S., where dengue, Zika and other Aedes aegypti mosquito-borne diseases occur," says Albert Icksang Ko, co-principal investigator of the trial and Raj and Indra Nooyi professor of public health at Yale University.

"The intervention substantially reduced dengue infections during Brazil's largest recorded outbreak, demonstrating its potential to protect communities even under conditions of intense transmission," adds Derek Cummings, co-principal investigator of the trial and Bloomberg distinguished professor at Johns Hopkins University.

Ozone device developed to tackle hidden source of hospital infections

A University of Glasgow spinoff has developed a handheld device that uses ozone generated from fresh air to tackle one of the most persistent and overlooked sources of hospital infection—contaminated sink drains.

Developed through more than 15 years of university research and now being commercialized by Glanadair, the latest version of the technology is a device that creates ozone on demand using only air and electricity and can be placed easily over a drain opening in a hospital sink.

Ozone is generated by the device inside the drain system, allowing it to reach bacteria hidden in areas that are difficult or impossible to clean using conventional methods such as bleach. Once treatment is complete, any remaining ozone is safely converted back into ordinary oxygen, leaving no chemical residue behind.

The Glasgow team believes using ozone, widely recognized as one of the most powerful disinfectants available, to target the root of drain contamination could help reduce the risk of health care-associated infections while reducing reliance on harsh chemical cleaning agents.

Declan Diver, a professor who co-founded Glanadair with Dr. Hugh Potts and is one of the inventors of the technology, said, "About 10% of patients who go into the hospital pick up another infection when they are there—and the source of that infection is the drains.

"Hospital drains can harbor harmful bacteria within biofilms that are very difficult to remove. Because ozone is a gas, it can penetrate those biofilms and reach places that liquid disinfectants often cannot.

"We essentially make disinfectant from fresh air. The challenge has always been how to generate and control ozone safely and effectively. That's what this device allows us to do."

The science underpinning the device is already well established. In a 2025 peer-reviewed study published in the Journal of Hospital Infection, researchers demonstrated that plasma-generated ozone significantly reduced bacterial contamination within drains while preventing ozone from escaping into the surrounding environment.

The research showed that ozone generated from ambient air could safely disinfect otherwise inaccessible drain systems and piping.

The technology builds on earlier University of Glasgow innovations that used ozone to extend the shelf life of fresh fruit and vegetables. Drawing on that experience, the team refined the underlying science and engineering to create a more powerful and practical system for infection-control applications.

Alongside its cleaning capabilities, the device can also record when a sink has been disinfected and by whom, creating a digital audit trail for hospital cleaning teams.

With a patent recently filed and now pending, the technology is being prepared for wider deployment and clinical workflow trials, with hospitals already expressing interest in evaluating the system.

Meanwhile, Glanadair is seeking investment to support manufacturing and has reached the final stages of the Scottish EDGE competition.

For Diver, the appeal of the technology lies in its simplicity. He said, "We're taking something that is freely available all around us, the air we breathe, and turning it into a powerful tool for infection prevention. If we can make hospitals safer using air, electricity and smart engineering, then that's a very exciting prospect."

Five months after the American Diabetes Association fractured over a political protest and its extended fallout, one question remains unanswered.

What’s the bottom line for people living with diabetes?

Although any impact on patients may be hard to trace now, experts told STAT, they expressed concern that the impasse could stymie advancement in diabetes care. At the heart of the matter is the role the ADA and other professional organizations play in setting guidelines and sharing research, whether in their journals or at wide-ranging meetings that attract thousands to present and to learn.

The ADA dispute began after five members were ousted from its 2026 scientific meeting in New Orleans. The sparring continues, fueled by high-profile resignations and dismissals, a 1,221-member boycott, and the appointment of unidentified editors to manage journals. In October, an internal ADA review acknowledged some missteps but doubled down on its rebukes of members who objected to Trump administration policies decimating scientific research and proposing political reviews of individual projects.

A scheduled appearance by Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, inspired the five members to pass out copies of an editorial published in an ADA journal critical of diminished NIH funding. He did not appear, but armed security officers evicted those who shared the printouts outside the hall where he was expected to speak.

Bhattacharya was not the speaker originally suggested for the meeting, Mark Atkinson, who resigned as ADA’s 2026 scientific sessions planning committee chair, told STAT. His choice was to assemble a panel of academic experts to discuss artificial intelligence and its influence on diabetes care, but ADA leadership and its advocacy committee selected Bhattacharya instead.

These and other details regarding the dispute have accumulated, along with high-level resignations. But when asked if the continuing controversy matters to patients, the answer from four prominent voices is yes, but maybe not yet.

To illustrate his concern for the ADA’s future, Atkinson cited examples of how the ADA helped patients in the past.

“The ADA is one of many agencies that have advocated for lower insulin costs,” he told STAT. “They’re one of many agencies that have argued for increased federal funding for research. They’re advocates for standards of care.”

David Nathan, a noted researcher and founder of the Diabetes Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, is far more concerned about the broader impact of federal funding cuts on the scientific enterprise than he is about ADA tumult. Still, he’s also hearing from people who link that ongoing national crisis to what has happened at ADA.

They’re afraid of what’s going to happen to diabetes research, he said, starting with the NIH withdrawing support and then aggravated by the ADA discord.

“It’s really one blow on top of another,” Nathan told STAT. “All of this has coalesced to make everyone anxious, uncertain about the future of diabetes research. And the ADA should at this point be standing up and being something that we can all rally behind. Instead it is being fractured by its own actions.”

In a written response to STAT’s request for comment, the ADA press team said Tuesday, “The ADA has outlined the next steps that we plan to take to learn and improve based on the facts that came to bear from the review. This includes a review of event protocols, procedures, and code of conduct.”

In the near term, the 2027 ADA guidelines to be issued in December were already close to completion, physicians familiar with their production told STAT. The ADA confirmed their publication online in Diabetes Care next month. The agenda for the next annual scientific sessions, slated for June in Washington, D.C., is not yet set.

Meanwhile, the journals have been in limbo.

Since June, the ADA member boycott has erased the editorial masthead for Diabetes Care, its flagship journal. Editor-in-chief Steven Kahn, one of the five escorted out this past June, is part of the boycott, as are deputy editors. Chris Kohler, vice president of publications at ADA, resigned in protest when an interim editorial board was appointed without making their names public.

Kohler’s resignation letter said the appointment of unidentified interim editors violated editorial independence, scientific integrity, transparency, and accountability.

item.title: Opinion: A Chinese research entity FOIA’d my scientific work. I had to give it to them
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Team science — or collaborative science across disciplines and institutions — is essential for scientific progress as modern problems are too complex for a single person, laboratory, or even field to solve alone. Some of the best work happens when scientists from different countries collaborate.

However, U.S. policies in place and in development increasingly curtail this vital foreign collaboration. There are foreign funding restrictions, visa and entry restrictions for researchers, mandatory institutional compliance and audits with respect to foreign collaborations, and tight export controls. These policies were implemented as biosecurity measures to protect from “countries of concern,” including China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Meanwhile, proprietary scientific research is easily accessible to anyone, including foreign actors, through a policy meant to protect Americans’ right to government information. In other words, we are locking the front door while the back window is still wide open.

How does this happen?

The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) is a U.S. federal law enacted in 1966 in response to concerns that the government was too broad and unaccountable. FOIA gives anyone the right to request access to records held by federal government agencies.

This means that through FOIA, anyone — U.S. citizens, noncitizens, and foreign nationals — can access U.S. government-funded science by completing a simple online form and paying a minimal fee. While FOIA is an incredibly important tool for citizens in a free society, it was never intended to allow anyone around the globe to access proprietary U.S. science.

People are readily climbing in through the open back window. As a scientist in the U.S., I personally experienced the impact of such a FOIA request. I was notified by a FOIA coordinator at an NIH institute that my scientific ideas, supported by a funded grant from the U.S. government, were being requested by a Chinese entity through a simple online request form. They only had to pay a $25 fee.

By law, I had to comply and release the grant to them. The requester was listed as a “Consultant” and identified by a generic email address and physical address in China that could not be verified.

I am not the only one to have this experience. The FOIA coordinator told me offhand that this specific individual had a track record of requesting numerous grants from different NIH institutes every year. More broadly, over a decade, the NIH received more than 13,300 requests for grant proposals through FOIA. (Meanwhile, journalists’ FOIA requests often face major delays and other hurdles.)

This loophole has significant negative ramifications on our society. Scientific grants contain unpublished scientific data and sensitive intellectual property. The release of this material could:

1) harm personal and institutional financial interests by divulging patentable ideas, product concepts, and precompetitive information;

2) mislead the public through exposure to unvetted and untested hypotheses and preliminary data;

3) ruin careers and livelihoods of U.S. scientists; and perhaps most importantly,

4) damage U.S. interests by allowing foreign nationals or foreign corporations to be the primary beneficiaries of work funded by the U.S. taxpayer.

Our policies are fundamentally not aligned to protect science. We say we are blocking competing foreign interests, yet through FOIA, anyone can access this science.

If the U.S. truly wants to protect science, Congress needs to close the open window that FOIA affords. Proprietary U.S. science should be exempt or excluded from FOIA. Failing that, those who can access our material must be scrutinized.

Almost exactly four years after receiving the FOIA request, a research team from China published findings that closely matched my team’s original hypothesis — one our own later experiments did not support. While I cannot say whether the FOIA request, my grant, and this recent publication are related, the timing has made me think more about how research, including my own, is ultimately used in these situations.

Francesca E. Duncan, Ph.D. is the Thomas J. Watkins memorial professor of reproductive science in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology in the Feinberg School of Medicine at Northwestern University. She is also an associate professor in residence at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging. The views presented here are her own.

item.title: Opinion: If the AI bubble bursts, it could create a serious problem for health care
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The Oct. 30 sell-off on Wall Street ignited doubts about whether the huge investment in artificial intelligence will earn the returns investors expect. Those concerns have persisted, with even Anthropic’s initial public offering on Nov. 19 failing to halt the broader tech sell-off.

If the AI bubble bursts (assuming it is a bubble) and takes some medical AI companies down with it, health care will face a serious problem. A health AI company’s market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things. If funding runs out because investors decide to walk away, hospitals could lose the chance to complete evaluations of potentially useful medical tools. Giving up on medical AI would be a financial decision — but it may look like a clinical one. The financial markets will decide which medical AI technologies survive before hospitals have had the opportunity to establish whether these technologies benefit patients.

If investment in medical AI technologies experiences a sharp fall, companies will lose funding, forcing them to reduce their activities or stop supporting their technologies completely. The impact of such an event could be felt across the entire health care system: Companies are developing AI tools ranging from interpreting scans to identifying patients at risk of developing medical complications due to treatments. Clearly, some of these tools will eventually prove useful in clinical settings, while others will not. The point is that neither an impressive AI tool nor a falling stock price tells us which AI tool deserves a place within the health care system.

To illustrate this point, let’s take cancer clinical trials as an example. In one study, researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Emory University examined electronic medical records using AI systems to identify patients who may meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in clinical trials. Determining eligibility involves a demanding manual screening process examining things like tumor characteristics, previous treatments, and lab results.

Interestingly, the findings revealed that using the AI system improved accuracy of assessing enrollment eligibility for the cancer clinical trials, but it didn’t reduce screening time significantly. It’s not clear whether such improvements would lead to an increase in patient enrollment. In another study, researchers in Australia from the Victorian Cancer Registry at Cancer Council Victoria and Monash Health utilized an AI system to analyze pathology reports with the goal of identifying patients eligible for enrollment in cancer clinical trials. The AI system was able to successfully identify more eligible patients when compared to standard screening procedures, but ultimately utilizing the AI system didn’t result in increased patient enrollment into the clinical trials. The study didn’t establish why, which brings to focus that screening improvements doesn’t necessarily lead to higher clinical trial participation.

Taken together, these two studies illustrate the potential utility of AI systems in health care. They also make clear that improvements are needed before such AI systems become an integral part of health care system.

Based on my experience in senior leadership in oncology drug development, I think that medical AI systems should be developed and evaluated based on the general framework that we currently apply in the research and development of new innovative cancer drugs. What I mean by that is when it comes to the AI systems promising early results are important, but it is critical not to celebrate a success too early. Ultimately the value of the AI system depends on whether it eventually benefits the patient. We need to determine whether using a particular medical AI leads to better clinical decisions, better patient identification, reduction of unnecessary work, or improved access to treatment.

If the AI bubble bursts, these success metrics could become more difficult to achieve. Companies developing medical AI systems may lose their funding, downsize, or even withdraw support for their products. Worst of all, they could close before hospitals have finished assessing their AI systems.

Clinicians could, of course, return to doing their work as they did before the introduction of the medical AI system. But that would mean the health care system loses the opportunity (and valuable data) to determine whether such medical AI tools could have offered meaningful improvements and patient impact.

The clear answer is not to try and save each struggling AI company, but to make sure that hospitals and health care system are able to complete their assessments of medical AI systems even if a given company reduces its services or even goes out of business.

Before adopting such medical AI systems, hospitals should establish clear success criteria and build systems in place to track, store, and ensure that the research data generated about the medical AI systems are available for independent evaluation even if the AI company supporting such a system no longer exists. Such plans would make sure that any financial difficulties that may affect a relevant AI company would not prevent the hospital or the health care system from determining whether a given medical AI system could benefit patients.

David Adler is chief scientific officer at the PATHORA Institute of Pathology & Tissue Medicine, with more than 15 years of experience in oncology research and drug development.

item.title: Parcheo virtual vs. parcheo: cuándo proteger una API en lugar de redesplegarla
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

El parcheo virtual bloquea temporalmente una vía conocida para llegar a un fallo de software mientras el código vulnerable sigue en su sitio. Úsalo cuando puedas cubrir el tráfico de API afectado antes de lo que tardarías en desplegar una corrección de forma segura. Aplica el parche y verifica la flota afectada en cuanto la compilación corregida esté lista.

El 23 de noviembre de 2026, OpenAI y Cisco presentaron Shirudo, un proyecto Linux de código abierto que puede cargar protecciones eBPF específicas en un sistema en ejecución. Pone el foco en una decisión habitual para el equipo de guardia. Si la corrección permanente tarda horas en validarse, ¿puedes reducir la exposición ahora sin romper las solicitudes de las que dependen tus clientes? Anuncio de Shirudo de OpenAI

Parcheo virtual frente a parcheo convencional

Un parche virtual es un control compensatorio. Tu inventario sigue mostrando la versión vulnerable mientras el control está activo. Mantén abierto el ticket de remediación y registra allí la regla, el propietario y la fecha de retirada prevista. Guía de parcheo virtual de OWASP

Un parche convencional puede ser una biblioteca actualizada en una imagen de contenedor o una compilación corregida de tu propio servicio. Haz seguimiento de lo que realmente se está ejecutando en la flota. Una imagen corregida en el registro dice poco sobre los workers antiguos que siguen atendiendo solicitudes. Guía de gestión de parches empresariales de NIST

¿Cuándo conviene usar un escudo para una API?

Usa un escudo cuando se cumplan tres condiciones.

- El control cubre el tráfico afectado. Confirma qué rutas de entrada y cargas de trabajo están dentro del alcance, incluidos los llamadores internos y el procesamiento en segundo plano cuando corresponda.

- Puedes validarlo antes que la compilación corregida. Usa tráfico representativo de staging para comprobar el comportamiento previsto de la regla y confirmar que las solicitudes normales siguen funcionando.

- Alguien es responsable de la salida. Asigna el despliegue del parche, acuerda la evidencia de cobertura y fija una fecha de revisión para el cambio temporal.

Supongamos que una API de objetos tiene una función opcional de procesamiento vulnerable y que el gateway ya admite desactivar el acceso a esa función. Tu equipo puede evaluar rápidamente el comportamiento con esa función desactivada mientras vuelve a compilar y probar el servicio. Las lecturas de colección y de detalle deberían seguir funcionando. Si los clientes usan la función opcional, informa a soporte de qué respuesta recibirán esos clientes y cuánto tiempo es probable que dure el cambio.

Mide ambos lados del equilibrio. Compara el tiempo previsto para aplicar la regla con el tiempo necesario para llevar una compilación corregida al mismo conjunto de cargas de trabajo. Durante el despliegue, vigila el éxito de las solicitudes normales, la latencia y los recuentos de rechazos. Un aumento de los rechazos necesita contexto. Puede ser que el control esté haciendo su trabajo o que se trate de un flujo de trabajo de cliente que tus datos de prueba de staging no contemplaron.

Prioriza un parche inmediato cuando la compilación corregida esté lista, un despliegue canario tenga buen estado y el despliegue llegue a las instancias expuestas con la misma rapidez que la regla temporal. Si ningún control fiable cubre la ruta afectada y el riesgo justifica una actuación inmediata, considera restringir el acceso o desactivar la capacidad afectada mientras se prepara la corrección. Si tienes evidencia de compromiso, inicia la respuesta a incidentes junto con la remediación.

¿Dónde debe ejecutarse un escudo de API?

Elige el punto de aplicación según lo que pueda observar y qué solicitudes deben pasar por él. Un firewall de aplicaciones web (WAF) en un gateway de API evalúa allí el tráfico HTTP. Un escudo de tiempo de ejecución de Linux aplica la política donde el host puede observar la actividad relevante. Cada uno depende de la cobertura en su propia capa.

Una regla de gateway encaja en un cambio expuesto por HTTP cuando el gateway ve los atributos de solicitud relevantes y todas las solicitudes afectadas pasan por él. Verifica el alcance con el inventario de servicios. Si un servicio gestiona trabajo de varias fuentes, incluye esas rutas en tu plan de remediación. Para ver un ejemplo específico de dependencia sobre por qué importa el inventario de componentes, consulta nuestra cobertura de una vulnerabilidad de Node.js Brotli.

Un control en el host tiene sentido cuando el comportamiento relevante es visible en el host y puedes establecer cobertura en los kernels y las cargas de trabajo afectados. Su ubicación puede acercar el control al componente que proteges, con sus propios requisitos de despliegue y reversión. Mantén las comprobaciones de autorización de la aplicación en el plan de pruebas de lanzamiento. Un cambio en el gateway debe revisarse junto con cualquier cambio en la autorización de middleware.

¿Qué aporta Shirudo?

Shirudo puede cargar protecciones eBPF específicas en un sistema Linux en ejecución sin reiniciarlo para aplicar el escudo. OpenAI describe un flujo de trabajo asistido por agentes para preparar y comprobar un escudo candidato, con operadores que controlan el despliegue. item.title: It's 2 a.m. and the ONTAP Volume Is Offline: A Triage Runbook for the NetApp Certified Support Engineer Exam
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Your phone buzzes at 2:07 a.m. The alert says a database team can't write to its NFS share, and the share lives on an ONTAP cluster you have never logged in to. What do you type first?

That question is the whole point of the NetApp Certified Support Engineer exam (NS0-194, NCSE). It doesn't ask whether you can design a storage array. It asks whether you can walk up to a broken one, find the cause and fix it without making things worse. That's why it also makes a good runbook.

This post is that runbook. Each step maps to one of the six official exam domains, and every command is real ONTAP CLI you can run in a lab or a simulator. You get a better on-call routine and a study plan in one read.

What is the NetApp Certified Support Engineer exam?

The NS0-194 exam validates the skills of an engineer who supports NetApp ONTAP systems on site or remotely. According to NetApp's Support Engineer certification page, it tests general troubleshooting and root cause isolation, hardware replacement, documentation, node configuration, and software and firmware upgrades. NetApp recommends six to 12 months of hands-on experience.

The question count, time and passing score come from the NWExam syllabus page. The domains and experience level come from NetApp. Check the current price on Pearson VUE when you book, because published figures differ between sources.

The six domains are ONTAP OS, troubleshooting NetApp hardware and software, NetApp hardware, NetApp cloud data services, data protection, and Active IQ. The runbook below covers them in the order you'd meet them during a real incident.

Step 1: Is the cluster itself healthy?

Before you look at the volume, look at the ground it stands on. Many "storage is broken" tickets are really a node down, a failed takeover or a network port that went dark.

cluster1::> cluster show

cluster1::> system health status show

cluster1::> system health alert show

cluster1::> storage failover show

cluster show tells you whether every node is healthy and eligible. storage failover show tells you whether the HA pairs are in a normal state or whether one node has taken over its partner. If a takeover happened at 2:01 a.m., you already have a strong lead.

This is the habit the exam rewards: collect information before you change anything. The troubleshooting domain literally lists "How to collect and analyze information" as its first objective.

Step 2: What do disks, aggregates and volumes say?

Next, go one layer up the stack, from physical disks to the aggregate to the volume.

cluster1::> storage disk show -broken

cluster1::> storage aggregate show -fields state,raidstatus

cluster1::> volume show -state offline

cluster1::> volume show -fields percent-used,available -percent-used >90

A quick refresher on the ONTAP OS domain's "disk or aggregate concepts" and "volume concepts":

- Disks are grouped into RAID groups, and RAID groups make up an aggregate.

- An aggregate is the pool of physical capacity on one node.

- FlexVol volumes are carved out of an aggregate and owned by a storage VM (SVM).

- An aggregate in a degraded RAID state still serves data, but losing another disk could take it down.

If the volume is offline and you know why (for example, someone took it offline for maintenance and forgot), bring it back:

cluster1::> volume online -vserver svm_db -volume vol_db01

If it's online but 100% full, writes fail even though nothing is "down". That's one of the most common causes of a "can't write" ticket. Check whether snapshot reserve or a runaway log file is eating the space before you grow the volume.

Step 3: Can the client actually reach the data LIF?

ONTAP serves data through logical interfaces (LIFs) that sit on physical or virtual ports. After a takeover or a cable problem, a LIF can end up on a port that isn't its home port, or on a port with no link at all.

cluster1::> network port show -link down

cluster1::> network interface show -is-home false

cluster1::> network interface show -vserver svm_db -fields address,home-node,curr-node,status-oper

If the LIFs migrated and the home ports are healthy again, send them back:

cluster1::> network interface revert -vserver svm_db -lif *

This is the "ONTAP networking concepts" objective in practice. Know the difference between a physical port, an interface group, a VLAN and a broadcast domain, and know that a LIF fails over within its failover group.

Step 4: Is the client allowed in?

The network is fine and the volume is online, but the client still gets "permission denied". Now you're in the "How to troubleshoot data access problems" objective, which comes up a lot.

For NFS, ONTAP has a built-in command that evaluates the export policy for you. You give it the client IP, protocol and access type, and it shows you which rule matched at every level of the path:

cluster1::> vserver export-policy check-access -vserver svm_db -volume vol_db01 -client-ip 10.20.30.41 -authentication-method sys -protocol nfs3 -access-type read-write

If the result says read where you expected read-write, or denied, look at the rule index it names:

cluster1::> vserver export-policy rule show -vserver svm_db -policyname db_hosts

Common causes are a client match that names the wrong subnet, rw set to never, or a parent junction with a stricter policy than the volume. The check-access output shows each path component, so a parent problem stands out.

For SMB, name resolution and domain connectivity cause most failures:

cluster1::> vserver services name-service dns check -vserver svm_files

cluster1::> vserver cifs show -vserver svm_files

The exam's "Supported ONTAP protocols" and "How ONTAP interacts with external components" objectives cover this: DNS, LDAP, Active Directory, NTP and the clients themselves.

Step 5: Is it slow rather than broken?
