Patching Virtual vs Patching Biasa untuk API: Kapan, Di Mana, dan Kapan Dihapus

Patching virtual untuk sementara memblokir jalur yang diketahui menuju celah perangkat lunak saat kode rentan masih berada di tempatnya. Gunakan saat Anda dapat menjangkau lalu lintas API yang terdampak lebih cepat daripada Anda dapat men-deploy perbaikan dengan aman. Patch dan verifikasi fleet yang terdampak begitu build perbaikan siap.

Pada 23 November 2026, OpenAI dan Cisco memperkenalkan Shirudo, proyek Linux open-source yang dapat memuat proteksi eBPF yang ditargetkan pada sistem yang sedang berjalan. Proyek ini menyoroti keputusan on-call yang sudah lazim. Jika perbaikan permanen membutuhkan waktu berjam-jam untuk divalidasi, dapatkah Anda mengurangi eksposur sekarang tanpa merusak permintaan yang diandalkan pelanggan? Pengumuman Shirudo dari OpenAI

Patching virtual vs patching biasa

Patch virtual adalah kontrol kompensasi. Inventaris Anda masih menampilkan versi rentan selama kontrol aktif. Biarkan tiket remediasi tetap terbuka dan catat aturan, pemilik, serta tanggal penghapusan yang diperkirakan di sana. Panduan patching virtual dari OWASP

Patch biasa dapat berupa library yang diperbarui dalam image container atau build layanan Anda sendiri yang telah diperbaiki. Lacak apa yang benar-benar dijalankan fleet. Image yang telah diperbaiki di registry tidak banyak menjelaskan tentang worker lama yang masih melayani permintaan. Panduan manajemen patch enterprise dari NIST

Kapan Anda perlu melindungi API?

Gunakan perisai saat tiga kondisi berikut terpenuhi.

- Kontrol mencakup lalu lintas yang terdampak. Pastikan jalur ingress dan workload mana yang termasuk dalam cakupan, termasuk pemanggil internal dan pemrosesan latar belakang bila relevan.

- Anda dapat memvalidasinya lebih cepat daripada build perbaikan. Gunakan lalu lintas staging yang representatif untuk memeriksa perilaku aturan yang dimaksud dan memastikan permintaan normal tetap berfungsi.

- Ada yang bertanggung jawab atas jalan keluarnya. Tetapkan rollout patch, sepakati bukti cakupan, dan tentukan waktu tinjauan untuk perubahan sementara.

Misalnya, API objects memiliki fitur pemrosesan opsional yang rentan, dan gateway sudah mendukung penonaktifan akses ke fitur tersebut. Tim Anda dapat menilai perilaku saat dinonaktifkan dengan cepat sambil membangun ulang dan menguji layanan. Pembacaan collection dan detail harus tetap berfungsi. Jika pelanggan menggunakan fitur opsional tersebut, beri tahu tim support respons apa yang akan diterima klien tersebut dan berapa lama perubahan ini kemungkinan berlangsung.

Ukur kedua sisi trade-off. Bandingkan perkiraan waktu untuk menegakkan aturan dengan waktu untuk mendapatkan build perbaikan ke kumpulan workload yang sama. Pantau keberhasilan permintaan normal, latensi, dan jumlah penolakan selama rollout. Kenaikan penolakan perlu konteks. Bisa jadi itu kontrol yang menjalankan tugasnya, atau alur kerja pelanggan yang terlewat oleh fixture staging Anda.

Utamakan patch langsung saat build perbaikan sudah siap, canary terlihat sehat, dan rollout menjangkau instance yang terekspos secepat aturan sementara. Jika tidak ada kontrol tepercaya yang mencakup jalur terdampak dan risiko menuntut tindakan segera, pertimbangkan membatasi akses atau menonaktifkan kemampuan yang terdampak selama perbaikan disiapkan. Jika Anda memiliki bukti kompromi, mulai respons insiden bersamaan dengan remediasi.

Di mana sebaiknya perisai API dijalankan?

Pilih titik penegakan berdasarkan apa yang dapat diamati dan permintaan mana yang harus melewatinya. Web application firewall (WAF) di gateway API mengevaluasi lalu lintas HTTP di sana. Perisai runtime Linux menerapkan kebijakan di tempat host dapat mengamati aktivitas yang relevan. Masing-masing bergantung pada cakupan di lapisannya sendiri.

Aturan gateway cocok untuk perubahan yang menghadap HTTP ketika gateway melihat atribut permintaan yang relevan dan setiap permintaan yang terdampak melewatinya. Verifikasi cakupan terhadap inventaris layanan Anda. Jika suatu layanan menangani pekerjaan dari berbagai sumber, sertakan jalur tersebut dalam rencana remediasi Anda. Untuk contoh spesifik dependensi tentang mengapa inventaris komponen penting, lihat liputan kami tentang kerentanan Node.js Brotli.

Kontrol host masuk akal ketika perilaku yang relevan terlihat di host dan Anda dapat menetapkan cakupan di seluruh kernel dan workload yang terdampak. Penempatannya dapat membawa kontrol lebih dekat ke komponen yang Anda lindungi, dengan persyaratan rollout dan rollback tersendiri. Pertahankan pemeriksaan otorisasi aplikasi dalam rencana pengujian rilis. Perubahan gateway harus berada dalam tinjauan yang sama dengan perubahan apa pun pada otorisasi middleware.

Apa yang ditambahkan Shirudo?

Shirudo dapat memuat proteksi eBPF yang ditargetkan pada sistem Linux yang sedang berjalan tanpa memulai ulang sistem untuk menerapkan perisai. OpenAI menjelaskan alur kerja berbantuan agen untuk menyiapkan dan memeriksa calon perisai, dengan operator yang mengendalikan deployment. Proyek ini menjelaskan loader bertanda tangan untuk proteksi BPF, verifikasi kernel, dan bukti yang didukung TPM atas perubahan pada proteksi yang dimuat. Repositori Shirudo

Repositori tersebut menyebut proyek ini sebagai pra-rilis. Proyek ini mencantumkan kernel Linux dengan ABI signed-loader dan patch kernel Shirudo, ditambah TPM 2.0, untuk target produksi. OpenAI menggambarkan identifikasi dan deployment berskala besar di seluruh organisasi sebagai tujuan jangka panjang. Anggarkan secara terpisah untuk menyiapkan host dan meninjau perubahan sementara. Penjelasan OpenAI tentang peta jalan Shirudo…

The advent of the new Magic 9 Pro Max is a chance for the Chinese giant to, as usual, tell the world about how it's once again redefined mobile cinematography. It's the first proper Honor flagship — and second only to the Robot Phone — to benefit from its partnership with Arri. If you're unfamiliar, the German giant makes the Alexa cinema camera, which has shot at least six films which went on to win an Academy Award for cinematography. If nothing else, if your Instagram reel doesn't at least garner a nomination, you know it's not the hardware's fault.

The Magic 9 Pro Max is the first Honor flagship to use the company's new industrial design first seen on its lower-end N series models. That includes a new camera plateau, albeit with a new color contrast back panel around the frame which puts me in mind of... something. Similarly, this is the first Honor flagship to get the Pro Max moniker, a suffix I don't think I've seen elsewhere in the rest of the mobile industry, but which sounds so cool that you think it might inspire copycats.

Nestled inside, you'll find a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 system-on-chip with either 12GB or 16GB RAM and the choice of 256GB, 512GB or 1TB storage. Up front, it's packing a 6.8-inch, 2,868 x 1,320 LTPO OLED display with a 1-120Hz refresh rate and 10,000 nits peak brightness. That's paired with an 8,000mAh battery which can support up to 100W wired or 80W wireless charging. Rounding out the useful specs are Wi-Fi 7, space for two SIM cards as well as an eSIM and a 55-megapixel front-facing camera.

Of course, these are all just supporting players for the main event, the Arriflex-inspired triple camera system 'round back. It's equipped with a 200-megapixel, f/1.57 OIS primary lens and a 200-megapixel f/2.6 OIS telephoto, as well as a 50-megapixel f/2.0 ultra-wide camera. Of note is that Honor claims the primary lens has "gimbal" levels of optical stabilization to keep your shots as smooth as possible, no matter how you old it.

To make use of all those megapixels, Honor is launching its first dedicated imaging processor, the H1, and grabbed plenty of Arri's know-how. Honor says the Magic 9 Pro Max uses an end-to-end cinematic workflow, shooting high-end video in Arri LogC3 — the company's version of Log — as well as a series of Arri-created filters and color profiles you can apply to your footage. You'll have a pick of up to 87 Arri looks to apply to your footage, and you can even shoot in Cinema ratios like 2.39:1.

To further bolster its credentials in this arena, Honor is launching a series of accessories in partnership with SmallRig. Equip your phone with the SmallRig camera cage and you'll be able to attach it to either the Honor-branded Teleconverter G200 or the Teleconverter G500. They'll increase the phone's focal length by either 200mm or 500mm, enabling you to shoot distances you'd struggle to capture with AI-enhanced imaging.

Honor's Magic 9 Pro Max is debuting in Malaysia, priced at RM 5,999 (approx $1,455) for the 12GB RAM / 512GB storage option. It'll arrive in the Middle East next month, and take its first bow in the West at some point in January.

item.description:

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.

Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.

Every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.

He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

On failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.

For team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.

Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.

Aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.

In 2002 Gwynne Shotwell had a lunch that would change her life—and the trajectory of the business world as we know it. Then 38, she had been working for a decade at a rocket startup, frustrated at the pace of innovation on the ground. “It wasn’t a vibrant industry, and we hadn’t gotten back to the moon [in 30 years],” she said on a podcast in 2022. “The systems were designed to eliminate risk, so they took forever and cost too much.” A former colleague had just departed for another rocket startup, and she met him to celebrate at a favorite Austrian restaurant in the coastal L.A. suburb of El Segundo. Afterward, her friend suggested Shotwell stop by his new company to meet the owner.

The owner, of course, was Elon Musk. Fresh off making a fortune at PayPal, Musk laid out his vision to the curious Shotwell: make rockets a lot more cheaply than NASA; sell launches to commercial satellite companies at super-bargain prices; slash prices even more by making the rockets reusable. Shotwell blurted out that he needed a “business developer,” effectively a sales leader who could win the pre-product contracts needed to fund the vision. Musk called her with an offer, and within days, Shotwell came aboard SpaceX. “I knew that working for Elon would be my last job in aerospace,” she has often said.

The investors and funds that have bought shares in SpaceX since its debut as, pre-Anthropic, the biggest IPO of all time are placing a huge bet on the visionary genius of Elon Musk. Though they may not realize it, those investors are also betting on the far lesser-known figure who’s spent two decades at Musk’s side turning his seemingly crazy dreams into big-money ventures. Now 63, Shotwell was employee No. 7 at SpaceX, and the IPO made her extremely wealthy: her 12.6 million shares were worth some $2 billion after the company went public. While Musk is SpaceX’s CEO, chairman, and chief technology officer (and controls around 40% of the shares), Shotwell’s the operator. As she put it in a recent interview, “He focuses on the future…on strategy and deep dives on the technical [side]. I focus on things that are helpful to customers today to earn money.” Shotwell doesn’t post on social media or seek publicity. She toils behind the scenes, mining Musk’s portfolio of futuristic ideas for the ones she can craft into cash-generating products.

Shotwell has achieved a spectacular record of tackling never-before-seen technological hurdles. She oversaw development of the Falcon 9, the world’s first orbital-class reusable commercial rocket, and helped make SpaceX the first private company to carry astronauts into orbit. Her cost breakthroughs enabled the Starlink galaxy of over 11,000 satellites, now SpaceX’s prime revenue and profit provider. Douglas Loverro, a former top official in the Air Force space program who’s worked extensively with Shotwell, told Fortune that for decades he’s believed that the only thing that makes money in space is communications and connectivity. “Elon and Gwynne saw it,” he observes. “Gwynne made it happen.”

But Shotwell’s job just got exponentially more difficult. Musk has rebranded SpaceX as an AI company, taken it public, and forecast a $1 trillion revenue run rate by 2030, a feat he plans to achieve largely by putting data centers in orbit. To get there, SpaceX more than tripled its capex to $48.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, and in August Shotwell unveiled a $100 billion Louisiana launch site to send them up. Skeptics, including some who won’t bet against Musk, doubt the economics can ever work. The numbers, observes Aswath Damodaran, a professor at NYU’s Stern School of Business, are “mind-blowingly large.” His biggest fear for SpaceX’s future is that “it overspends on orbital AI.”

The biggest thing working in Shotwell’s favor is that she has mastered a challenge that has defeated many others: managing Musk himself. As Walter Isaacson states in his definitive biography Elon Musk, the boss “doesn’t naturally partner with people. Collegiality is not part of his skill set. He inspires, frightens, bullies, and does not like to share power.” At Tesla, for example, Musk named one president who served just over two years, and never replaced him. Somehow, Shotwell’s rare combination of an engineering mindset, a knack for smoothly wooing customers, not to mention her money-making instincts, has fully captured Musk’s confidence.

People who’ve observed the pair in action credit Shotwell as the adult in the next cubicle. “I’ve worked with both Elon and Gwynne, and I’ve got to tell you, working with Gwynne is a lot more pleasant,” says one former client. As Isaacson told Fortune, “Gwynne’s indispensable to SpaceX, a perfect mind partner for Elon. She knows how to accomplish his goals while occasionally altering his trajectories and being engineering-honest with him, which is the way he likes to operate. She combines an engineering mind with a fingertip feel for how to deal with people.”

It’s a kind of odd-couple collaboration that works. Tom Mueller, SpaceX’s first employee and developer of the Merlin engine that powers the Falcon rockets, said in an email to Fortune that Shotwell brought a “unique skillset to the table that complements all the talent Elon was assembling.” In other interviews Mueller, who retired from SpaceX in 2020, put it even more simply: “I built the rockets, but Gwynne built the company.”

For 24 years Musk has supplied the vision, and Shotwell’s genius has been finding the money. Now she has to monetize the most expensive idea he’s ever had. The question is, Can she? Can anyone?…

item.title: On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant financial issue affecting Social Security recipients, with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

Smaller checks lose a bigger share of the raise

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

By recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

The COLA is already behind inflation

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”

Seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

By then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

A 2032 shortfall looms over every future raise

Against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”

That job falls to the new Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t plan on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office.

In hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press.

Two franchises, two very different audiences

Both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games, meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

Like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’ young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

The opening-weekend audience bears out the split. Women made up 67% of ticket buyers and 74% were between 18 and 34, according to the AP. Lionsgate studied the risks of opening against GTA from the earliest stage of dating the film and concluded the two could coexist.

While the Mature-rated GTA VI may have kept men of a certain age glued to their consoles this weekend, the PG-13 Sunrise on the Reaping held onto the core Hunger Games crowd: young women, along with teens too young to play the game.

That base may also have come out of thirst for a big-screen, four-quadrant blockbuster. This fall has been a sleepy season for PG-13 action movies, with dramas, documentaries, and R-rated fare dominating the box office and the zeitgeist. Audiences liked what they found: the film earned an A- CinemaScore, up from the B+ that greeted Songbirds & Snakes.

The rest of the box office nearly doubled

Overall, the weekend was a surprisingly strong one for theaters. Total domestic grosses topped $160 million, nearly double the prior weekend, though still about 10% below the same frame last year, when Wicked: For Good opened.

Sunrise on the Reaping accounted for most of that. Behind it on the weekend chart came I Play Rocky with $9.3 million in its first weekend of wide release, Ebenezer at $7.7 million, and The Cat in the Hat at $6.9 million. You Can See Everything is still hanging in the top 10, adding another $2.5 million.

These titles are diverse, but most target an audience different from GTA VI. Beyond The Hunger Games locking up young women, I Play Rocky is for the boomer dads and The Cat in the Hat is for kids.

The game still dwarfs the movies

None of it came close to GTA VI. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, says the game’s day-one retail sales, including preorders, reached $3.79 billion worldwide, more than 20 times the weekend’s entire domestic box office.

Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.

The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market â individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?

'Very industrial and very unpersonal'

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions â be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.

Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]â¦ is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.

"They just look like big, money-grabbing deals," he says.

In Cardiff, Grainger, the UK's largest listed BTR developer, is currently offering a fully-furnished studio flat on the 20th floor of The Copper Works in the city centre with views over the bay for Â£1,265 a month.

It's a lot more than what is currently on offer on Rightmove, a 15 minute walk away from the city centre â a fully-furnished, ground-floor, one-bedroom flat with a garden for Â£800 a month.

But tenants in The Copper Works have free access to a gym, a cinema room, a roof terrace, and a games room. There's also free WiFi, a concierge service with a helpline, and other amenities. In addition, the studio flat has an EPC B rating as opposed to an EPC C rating for the one-bedroom flat down the road.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns Â£32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending Â£250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.

Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network.

She pays $2,250 (Â£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing.

"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Jess Baker, a UK chartered psychologist, says the appeal of such providers is understandable.

"Otherwise, the cognitive load can lead to feelings of being overwhelmed, excess worry and exhaustion."

【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explains the factors behind the drop in gas prices, with useful vocabulary and context.

The average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that’s 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only hace to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices.

“The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “But, given how things have developed, it’s not really a shock.”

So, why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It’s a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn’t any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump’s actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:

More oil exports are exiting the Middle East, including from the now-infamous Strait of Hormuz

Despite some ongoing conflict, the combination of U.S. naval escorts, complicated oil tanker transfers, and pipeline bypass routes have allowed the Middle East to return to nearly 90% of its pre-war oil exports, even though prices remain elevated from high tanker contracting and insurance costs. The rising levels of oil exports—despite depleted strategic oil reserves worldwide—have helped the global oil benchmark dip slightly below $90 per barrel as of Monday.

Trump has downplayed any large escalation of military conflict since the midterm elections and the blue wave of Democratic wins

Prior to the elections, Trump openly said he was delaying any major ramp-up in attacks until after the midterms. That warning was keeping oil prices inflated as oil markets anticipated more disruptions to global oil flows in November. While risks remain and no peace deal seems on the near-term horizon, the lack of an escalation has helped prices fall. “The biggest thing now is this looming uncertainty over whether there will be something concrete and long-lasting,” De Haan told Fortune.

Fuel prices almost always dip seasonally heading deeper into the fall and winter

From a simple supply-and-demand standpoint, fuel prices typically peak in the summer during the busy driving season and bottom out in the winter when more people are bundled up at home. Although there are brief travel spikes for Thanksgiving and Christmas, driving is typically muted near the end and beginning of each calendar year. Likewise, fuel is cheaper to manufacture during the colder months. Summer-grade gasoline is more expensive because of extra additives required to keep fuel components from evaporating in the heat. Winter-grade fuel is cheaper and less complex.

Refinery operations in the U.S. and worldwide kept prices inflated in September and October

Globally, nearly 10% of refineries remain offline, largely in the Middle East and Russia because of wars. But, in the U.S., there also were supply disruptions at ExxonMobil’s Joliet and Phillips 66’s Wood River refineries in Illinois. Those temporary outages from weather issues and mechanical failures caused additional price spikes throughout the Midwest. “The refining issues were boosting prices ahead of the election,” De Haan said. “As these issues have been getting resolved, they’ve been pushing prices down, coupled with the seasonality, coupled with oil markets.” Outside of the Middle East and Russia, China also had mothballed some refineries during the Iran war. As China has depleted more of its own reserves, the country has of late ramped up its output, including its fuel exports, adding to global supplies.

Refineries maximized their output of diesel this fall, which also means more gasoline

Refining complexes aren’t built to operate like light switches for diesel or other petroleum products. When refineries are pushed to run at their maximum utilization levels for diesel, that also means increasing their volumes of gasoline. With diesel demand surging in the fall, the U.S refining industry is on overdrive and raking in record profits, often delaying planned maintenance work until next year. “Refineries are operating at their highest November rate since 1998,” De Haan said. “This may be the highest utilization year for refineries ever. It’s going to be really close.”

Fuel prices remain elevated, but there’s no hiding how far they’ve fallen. As such, nearly as many Americans as last year plan to travel for Thanksgiving. AAA projects 72.9 million people will travel on the road this Thanksgiving, only a slight drop from 73.1 million last year.

GasBuddy’s survey data showed that almost two-thirds of Americans plan to hit the road this week. Close to 20% of travelers said they will cut back on other holiday spending to cover the extra fuel costs.

If there are no more major energy disruptions in the Middle East, De Haan said, the national average for gasoline could bottom out as low as $3.35 per gallon over the next few weeks.

Asian stocks rallied on Tuesday after the board of Nvidia—the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom—voted Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership crisis that had battered the region’s AI supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), which makes Nvidia’s chips, surged 9.9%, the daily limit, adding 5.2 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($158 billion) to its market value in a single day.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 3.9% as the market returned from a three-day weekend, while South Korea’s KOSPI surged 6.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX climbed 9%.

Tuesday’s rally marks a rebound after a brutal stretch for the AI trade. The TAIEX fell by 17.5% last week, its worst such drop since 1991, pushing regulators to impose market stabilization measures, such as banning short selling, over the weekend.

Foxconn and Wistron, which assemble AI servers around Nvidia’s chips, rose almost 10%. SK Hynix, the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, climbed 6.7%, while Samsung Electronics rose 6.6%. In Japan, Kioxia, Toshiba’s former memory chip unit, surged 10.0%, and Advantest, which makes chip-testing equipment, jumped 12.5%.

“This looks like a powerful relief rally, amplified by short covering and the sharp selloff that preceded it,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank, says. “The initial rebound could extend over the next few trading sessions, particularly in semiconductor-heavy markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, where earnings visibility has improved following [Jensen] Huang’s return.”

Yet the relief from Huang’s return will likely peter out as broader concerns about the AI ecosystem persist. “I would expect markets to become more selective over the coming weeks, as investors shift their focus back from Nvidia’s leadership to AI spending, earnings delivery and the Fed’s policy outlook,” Chanana adds.

Not every Asian market is having a good day. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index fell by 0.6%. “The Hang Seng and mainland Chinese markets have struggled to find support,” says Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, a currency and derivatives broker. “Without a meaningful rotation back into Chinese AI and technology stocks, sustained upside looks challenging.”

Huang’s return leaves export-control scrutiny unresolved

Huang’s return comes less than two weeks after his resignation. He stepped down on Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who some U.S. intelligence officials believed was working with Chinese espionage, according to the New York Times.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is at the center of allegations that Nvidia chips were diverted to China. The company has denied the allegations.

Last week, the Commerce Department expanded export controls on AI processors to Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and Brazil; it also closed a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia chips housed overseas.

On Monday, the department added seven companies to its Entity List, including Megaspeed. In a Federal Register notice, the department said the companies posed a “significant risk” and acted contrary to the “national security or foreign policy interests” of the U.S. The added companies include firms in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore, including several Megaspeed affiliates.

The same day, Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said in a statement.

item.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Dependent on Fossil Fuels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: comprehensive analysis with clear reporting and useful vocabulary

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India and southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño, the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.…

Why it is here: local issue with global implications, well-reported

- Plans to build a floating LNG storage facility off eastern Bali continue to attract opposition from affected communities on the Indonesian island.

- Civil society organizations have also criticized the planned development, pointing to tandem plans to develop vast solar energy capacity that have yet to be advanced.

- Local officials argue that higher demand for electricity necessitates building infrastructure to ensure reliable electricity, but campaigners say this will lock in greenhouse gas emissions in conflict with marketing efforts to portray the island as a green holiday destination.

DENPASAR, Indonesia — Customary leaders from Serangan village in Bali have renewed local opposition to a planned liquefied natural gas terminal off the east coast of the Indonesian island, saying the floating LNG site is too close to customary fishing grounds.

“We disagree with the 3.5-kilometer distance [2.2 miles] because the vessel is large, and very close to the village’s sacred point as well as our fishing routes,” said I Nyoman Gede Pariartha, the traditional leader in Serangan, at a meeting on Nov. 14.

Earlier this year Indonesia’s environment ministry issued an environmental permit for a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) off the eastern coast of Serangan island in Bali. The new infrastructure is intended to improve the reliability of Bali’s electricity supply by supplying gas-fired power plants amid rising electricity demand on the island.

Bali has a population of 4.5 million, but the island received almost 7 million tourism visits in 2025 and, since the pandemic, has increasingly been host to longer-term visitors.

Increasing electricity demand on the island is supplied by several power plants on Bali, including the gas-fired Pesanggaran power station, a 200 megawatt capacity facility next to a protected mangrove forest on the northern fringe of Benoa Bay.

In addition, up to 30% of the island’s electricity is supplied by cables from neighboring Java, the world’s most populous island.

The planned new FSRU site east of Bali will receive liquified natural gas offshore from tankers, and convert the fuel back into natural gas before supplying it through pipelines to Pesanggaran power station.

However, the new FSRU location has previously been moved from another site in Sidakarya village amid local opposition in an area with a history of grassroots resistance to large-scale development.

In 2013, a proposal backed by an oligarch to reclaim hundreds of hectares of the bay for luxury resorts, hotels and entertainment facilities met with opposition.

Artists, civil society, customary village leaders and students coalesced under a broad movement to protect Benoa Bay’s mangroves, marine ecosystems, livelihoods and sacred sites. The proposal was eventually shelved after years of campaigning.

Greenpeace action

Greenpeace activists floated a banner in Benoa Bay in the shape of a sea turtle saying “No Fossil Gas in Paradise” ahead of COP31 in Turkey, which ended on Nov. 22 without a new agreement on fossil fuels to prevent breakdown of global climate.

“We are witnessing how the climate crisis is fueling disasters that are intensifying and worsening year after year,” said Iqbal Damanik, climate and energy manager at Greenpeace Indonesia. “All of these climate-related disasters are driven by the use of fossil fuels.”

“Adding LNG facilities in southern Bali will shrink fishing grounds, destroy mangrove ecosystems, and harm sea turtle habitats,” said Greenpeace Indonesia lead Yuyun Harmono. “Stop using fossil gas and shift focus immediately to renewables.”

Indonesia is struggling to overcome structural limitations to the energy transition due to a surplus of independent coal producers given lucrative take-or-pay contracts to supply the Java-Bali grid, which serves a majority of the population in the world’s fourth-largest country.

In effect, coal plants are paid to burn coal whether or not Indonesia’s national grid, PLN, buys the electricity.

The Institute Essential Services Reform, a think tank focused on energy, estimates total solar energy potential in Bali of up to 22 gigawatts, which is greater than the total installed capacity from all sources on Denmark’s national grid.

In 2025, Bali governor I Wayan Koster unveiled a new rooftop solar energy plan to help Bali achieve net zero emission by 2045, a target the governor announced in 2023. The government in Bali could not be reached for comment.

“Adding new fossil-fuel capacity will only prolong Indonesia’s entrapment in a fossil-fuel-dependent system and hinder the energy transition,” Yuyun said.

item.title: Indonesian Borneo’s forests go quiet as smoke silences gibbons. Their singing matters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique perspective on environmental impact with clear detail

- Researchers in Indonesian Borneo have observed that gibbons’ morning songs have been reduced or absent during this fire season, a pattern also observed during previous fires.

- Researchers have not yet formally analyzed their findings, but suspect a major driver is smoke, which irritates gibbons’ airways and reduces the light that cues morning duets.

- Longer term, researchers fear gibbons’ health and fertility will be reduced by habitat disturbances and loss of food caused by the fires.

- When gibbons sing less, it also complicates the work of researchers, who typically rely on monitoring songs to find and count the animals.

Around dawn, a gibbon pair starts to sing. Their voices interweave, and the duet builds to a crescendo that fills the canopy. Across much of the Bornean forest, this is the sound of the morning.

But since smoke from Indonesia’s worst fire crisis in over a decade has engulfed the island, forests have become noticeably quieter. On days when the haze is thick, the Borneo Nature Foundation (BNF) field team in Sebangau, Central Kalimantan, reports that gibbons sing less. Their songs sound shorter. Morning duets start later than usual, if they happen at all.

Susan Cheyne, BNF’s co-director and vice-chair of the IUCN Primate Specialist Group Section on Small Apes, documented a similar pattern following forest fires in the same area in 2006.

Researchers have yet to formally analyze their observations of the effects of this year’s fires, and will not be able to separate the different factors until the fires have subsided and fieldwork can resume. Cheyne believes several causes may be at play, with smoke — which irritates gibbons’ airways and reduces the light that cues morning duets — as a major driver.

Why gibbon song matters

Singing plays a central role in the social and reproductive lives of gibbons. Fiercely territorial, socially monogamous primates, they sing not only to attract mates, but also to defend their territory. Paired adults perform elaborate duets to demonstrate the strength of their bond and ward off neighboring groups. Their songs are remarkably sophisticated, following rhythmic patterns and note sequences in ways that primatologists have compared to human music and language.

For gibbons, singing demands considerable energy and coordination — it is “an honest signal biologically,” according to Cheyne. A complex, well synchronized duet is difficult to fake, serving as a reliable sign of a healthy, strongly bonded pair.

Gibbon vocal behavior is also sensitive to environmental conditions. Research has found that they appear to sing less when exposed to disturbances like rain and noise pollution.

How smoke disrupts morning duets

Since mid-September, air quality in Central Kalimantan, has frequently reached hazardous levels. In the capital, Palangkaraya, pollution levels in October peaked at 11,981, nearly four times the level the U.S. Air Quality Index classifies as hazardous. As of Nov. 2, the Indonesian Ministry of Health reported more than 400,000 cases of acute respiratory infections across Central Kalimantan and six other affected provinces.

Borneo is home to four species of gibbons, all of which are endemic and endangered. Like humans, they have been exposed to high concentrations of smoke particles. Cheyne expects the smoke to affect gibbons in similar ways, irritating their airways and making it harder to breathe. This is likely one of the driving factors behind the drop in singing.

“I’m sure an opera singer would never be able to hit the notes and range and frequency that they should be able to if they’re constantly breathing in smoke,” she says.

Smoke may also affect singing by reducing visibility and dimming the light inside the forest. An analysis of more than 300 days of gibbon singing data from northern Lao PDR found gibbons tend to sing later and less often on foggy mornings. Gibbons typically perform their duets around sunrise, as light starts to filter through the canopy.

“We think that light is the main cue,” Cheyne says. When haze obscures sunrise, gibbons may delay their singing or skip it altogether.

According to Cheyne, there is also a visual, acrobatic component to their territorial displays, which may help explain later starts on hazy days. “They’re not just sitting; they’re swinging and singing at the same time.”

Alasdair Owens, a post-graduate researcher at the University of Exeter in England who uses passive acoustic data to study Bornean white-bearded gibbons (Hylobates albibarbis), says a factor that may become more evident in coming months is the lasting effect of the fires on the availability of fruit, which makes up the bulk of gibbon diets. Food shortages, he says, could impact their singing.

Fires have burned across parts of the ranges of Borneo’s gibbons, including an estimated 13,000 hectares (32,100 acres) inside Sebangau National Park. Previous El Niño fires have led to what Owens describes as “almost famine conditions” in the forest.

A 2015 study on orangutans, gibbons’ larger relatives, found that females adjusted their behavior for months following forest fires and fruit shortages. They rested more and traveled less to reduce energy expenditure. Gibbons have also been found to sing less when food availability declines.

The longer-term effects of reduced singing on gibbons’ health, social relationships and reproductive success remain unclear. Cheyne predicts that if families sing less, neighbors might encroach on their territory, leading to conflict between groups, while young gibbons may struggle to find mates.

Disruptions to gibbons’ daily routines caused by haze and delayed morning duets could also have far-reaching consequences. If gibbons reduce their active hours, they may have less time to feed and socialize, Cheyne says.

item.description:

Why it is here: interesting case study with clear reporting

- Timor-Leste’s booming swim-with-whales tourism industry is seeing growing numbers of operators and increasingly aggressive practices, raising concerns about its impact on migrating pygmy blue whales.

- New official guidelines aim to protect whales, but repeated breaches have exposed the lack of enforcement in an industry with no formal regulatory framework —the government is aiming for regulations to be legally reviewed by next year.

- Disagreements between operators and scientists over how closely tourists can approach whales highlight the challenges of balancing commercial interests with animal welfare.

- Conservationists and operators want licensing, monitoring and limits on boat numbers, and greater participation from Timorese in an industry dominated by foreign firms.

DILI, Timor-Leste — As the annual whale migration gets into full swing in Timor-Leste, conservationists are raising concerns about increasingly aggressive tourist encounters with the world’s largest animals, despite new guidelines designed to protect them.

Whale tourism is booming in a country whose waters are known as a “superhighway” for marine mammals. Migrating pygmy blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus brevicauda) are the star attraction for tourists seeking the experience of a lifetime.

Though haze from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia made spotting whale spouts difficult in the earlier part of the season, industry-watchers have noticed a marked increase in the number of operators on the water this year.

By the end of October, however, fewer whales had passed through the Ombai-Wetar Strait, which lies off the northern coast of Timor-Leste. This is likely because El Niño and the positive Indian Ocean Dipole have brought cooler waters in the region, delaying the migration of the whales, says cetacean ecologist Professor Karen Edyvane, who, in the past decade, has monitored migrating pygmy blue whales in Timor-Leste’s waters.

This has meant more intense competition among whale tour operators to deliver experiences for customers, who pay $250-350 a day for the chance to swim with one of the few hundred pygmy blue whales that pass through each year.

Industry-watchers have noticed cowboyish practices in the busiest season yet. Boats cutting across whales’ paths, operators pursuing mothers with calves, too many swimmers in the water at once — one tourist was taken out to swim with a whale on a jet ski — are among the reported violations.

“We’ve seen the same bad behavior as in the last few years — just more of it with the new boats,” Tom Quinney, a photographer who on Nov. 12 documented nine boats chasing what was believed to be a pregnant whale off the coast of Dili, told Mongabay in a written message. Quinney’s drone footage captures tourists free-diving with the whale, swimming within a few meters of it, and another drone being flown just above its head.

These practices breach guidelines released on Sept. 30 by the Timorese government and nonprofit Conservation International, with assistance from the Australian government and technical input from whale experts, including Edyvane.

Swimming with whales can be conducted responsibly if science and evidence-based guidelines are followed, but poorly managed encounters can have serious consequences for the cetaceans, Edyvane says.

Disruptions from boats and swimmers posing for Instagram photographs can cause pygmy blue whales to expend energy that they need to complete their annual migration from Indonesia’s Banda Sea, through Timor-Leste, to Australia.

“Critically, many of the animals we see in Timor-Leste’s waters are nursing mothers and calves – animals which need to nurse and rest, without ongoing disturbance from tour boats,” Edyvane told Mongabay in a written message.

From her whale monitoring field research station in Subaun on Timor-Leste’s northern coast, Edyvane has documented pygmy blue whales that are underweight, with their ribs and vertebrae visible. She suspects ocean warming is disrupting the upwellings that sustain their food supply.

Whale tourism could provide a significant boost to Timor-Leste’s nascent tourism economy. But the industry will have no future if it disrupts the migration on which it depends, says Delio da Costa, project coordinator for the Solutions for Marine and Coastal Resilience in the Coral Triangle (SOMACORE) at Conservation International.

Da Costa was part of the team that developed the new guidelines, which are an expanded version of recommendations published in 2020. They establish rules for approaching whales, including minimum distances and speed limits, and prohibit operators from chasing animals or blocking their paths.

Monitoring the ‘sinners’

Despite repeated reports of breaches, there have been no apparent consequences for rogue operators. Timor-Leste lacks a formal regulatory framework for whale tourism, and no operator has been apprehended for misconduct in the decade since the industry emerged.

It also lacks a clear avenue for complaints, which are directed instead to a general tourism information phone number and email. The government says it has yet to receive any whale-related complaints through these channels.

But observers are increasingly calling out malpractice. Last December, toward the end of the 2025 season, photographer Ollie Clarke wrote an open letter to the industry after witnessing multiple operators flouting internationally recognized rules. He described a “race to the bottom” as new players flood the market.

Also in December 2025, Quinney documented six boats pursuing a mother pygmy blue whale and her calf off the coast of the city of Manatuto.

One of the most serious breaches this year involved a boat speeding into the path of a female pygmy blue whale and her calf. Drone footage taken by marine biologist Ywen Mieybégué, seen by Mongabay, identified the vessel as belonging to Timor Sunshine Divers, one of the country’s largest operators.…

Biologists can spend decades working in the Amazon without seeing a bush dog. A new study quantifies just how rare the wild canids are.

Writing in Canid Biology & Conservation, Robert Wallace and his colleagues at the Wildlife Conservation Society analyzed 25 years of camera-trap data from 97 sites across seven South American countries. In more than 2.1 million photographs, taken over 611,159 camera-trap nights, bush dogs (Speothos venaticus) appeared on just 12 occasions.

Jaguars (Panthera onca) turned up about 100 times as often, and ocelots nearly 280 times. Even the short-eared dog (Atelocynus microtis), so fleetingly rare that it’s been nicknamed the “ghost dog,” was recorded 50 times as often as the bush dog.

Bush dogs are found from Costa Rica to northeastern Argentina. They have short legs, weigh up to 7 kilograms (about 15 pounds), and sometimes hunt in packs of a dozen. In Brazil’s Cerrado, a single family group was found to occupy a home range of 140 square kilometers (54 square miles).

In the latest study, the researchers analyzed footage from cameras mostly set 40–50 centimeters (16-20 inches) above the ground to photograph jaguars, which may have been a little high for bush dogs. Yet they readily photographed pacas, rodents of much the same size and shape as bush dogs, on nearly 40,000 occasions. A pack of dogs should also be easier to photograph than a solitary animal.

The researchers estimate that there are well under one bush dog per 100 km2 (roughly three per 100 mi2) across much of the species’ range. In the Amazon, the figure could be as low as one per 350 km2 (three per 350 mi2). Much of the data come from relatively intact forests in the western Amazon.

Living in packs makes bush dogs susceptible to outbreaks of disease. Domestic dogs brought into forests by hunters or settlers can carry canine distemper, parvovirus, and rabies. An entire pack could succumb to an infection picked up from a domestic dog.

The bush dog’s classification as near threatened on the IUCN Red List dates to 2011. The authors are calling for a reassessment.

Mason & Fifth’s Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice New-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Salon-quality haircare at home sounds fantastic, doesn’t it? For precisely this reason, though, the number of competitors in this space is enormous. So if you’re launching a new brand, how do you convince people you’re worth investing in? That was the challenge facing Yungbld, an independent, female-owned branding and design studio based in Florida, when its founder was building a haircare startup called Vollie.

Yungbld set out to strike a perfect balance between premium and approachable. No mean feat, and they didn’t stop at a logo and a label.

“The founder came to us with an idea to ‘bottle the salon’ and a formula,” explains Laura Miller, founder and creative chief at Yungblud. “And we built the brand into a full visual universe spanning strategy, identity, packaging, product design, CGI and animation, launch imagery, and an immersive digital experience at vollieverse.com.”

The new brand evolved from a clever tagline: ‘Handle With Haircare’. It’s a neat play on the warning you’d typically see on fragile parcels, and beautifully sets up the tension the brand is built on. Namely, that haircare products are meant to be gentle by design, but powerful in performance.

“We developed the entire experience around the idea ‘Handle With Haircare’, using sleek forms, dreamy textures, soft shadows and a restrained palette to create something that feels both premium and emotionally warm,” says Laura.

Colour and type

That restraint shows most clearly in the colour system. Yungbld has limited the palette to three pastels—candy pink, lilac, and pale periwinkle—anchored by black and a cool grey.

In one of the launch images, the studio depicts this literally as a Pantone swatch strip held over a model’s face, listing 230 C, 2635 C, 2120 C, Black 7 C and Cool Gray 2 C.

To balance all that softness, the typography is based around heavy, chunky, all-caps sans-serif. Black and bold, it’s the perfect choice for the wordmark, a series of one-word campaign posters (Oiled, Glossed, Brushed, Stacked) and crossheads on the website.

Products and packaging

On launch, Vollie’s range features three products: Super Soft, a softening and strengthening hair mask; Dream Defender, a prepare-and-protect hair oil; and So Glazed, a resurfacing gloss.

Each gets its own pastel. All three share a cylindrical bottle with a ribbed cap and a pointed nozzle. The wordmark is moulded into the bottle in relief rather than printed.

Yungbld also designed products beyond the bottles, including a wide-tooth comb with the wordmark running down its spine and clear tinted zip pouches that show the bottles inside.

CGI and live action

The CGI work leans into that idea of ‘dreamy textures’, with generous use of pastel soft gradients. The live-action imagery, though, takes a different route: warm, grainy and purposely lo-fi; again, achieving a lovely visual balance.

Overall, this brand launch impressed me by its heady combination of confidence and scale.

It would have been tempting to launch Vollie with a brief Instagram teaser, and a nice bottle and not much else. Instead, Yungbld has come out guns blazing, crafting a full brand world where packaging, product, motion, photography, and web all benefit from a shared language.

It’s soft where it needs to be and bold where it counts… just like the haircare products themselves.

item.title: What’s the answer to a sea of lookalike AI brands? A fossilised typewriter, a flight delay and hand-drawn cave art
