Why it is here: Unique branding story, creative use of inspiration, and useful vocabulary

Here’s a riddle for you. When is a flight delay actually a good thing? When it gives you a bizarre but brilliant slice of inspiration for an identity project, of course.

This is exactly what went down when Amsterdam creative agency Verve flew to Helsinki to throw around some ideas with the founders of AI startup Zero. Stuck in the city with time to kill, the Verve team wandered into a small museum, the Amos Rex, which is known for its subterranean galleries topped by undulating, dome-like skylights. As part of its Generation 2026 exhibition, there was a piece by ceramic artist [Johan Urrutia], depicting a typewriter that had turned to stone.

“Extinct office technology: that was the story,” says creative director Walewijn den Boer. And this simple idea became the key to the visual identity they created for Zero.

“The old tools are turning to stone, and Zero is bringing the new ones,” says Walewijn. “The more you live an assignment, the richer your associations get, and the more personal the work becomes.”

The new identity dramatises this notion by treating Zero’s arrival as an extinction event. Legacy CRM is presented as a Stone Age world of cracked earth and fossilised tools. Zero is something so advanced it barely reads as technology at all. And the line “Make CRM history” ties everything together.

Story of evolution

CRM, which stands for Customer Relationship Management, is one of the oldest categories in business software and has long been dominated by two huge companies: Salesforce and HubSpot.

“What I love about Zero is that it’s a story of evolution,” says strategy director Eveline Koppejan. “Salesforce and HubSpot were once the challengers kicking against what came before and now, decades later, they’re the incumbents, and a new generation is ready to kick back. The brand gives Zero the conviction to say that out loud.”

Zero isn’t only up against the big names, though. A wave of AI-native rivals is springing up, and most share the same dark-mode, crypto-adjacent startup look. To separate Zero, Verve offered founders several different visual territories, from an anti-brand rebellion to a safer lifestyle-tech route, but the extinction event won out.

“Compared with the other AI-native players, the product gap is slim, because everybody copies each other’s features and that’s easy to do now,” says Walewijn. “When the product becomes a chat interface, there’s no feature or screenshot left to hide behind. Brand is what differentiates.”

Visually, they’ve really taken the idea and run with it. A hand-illustrated Neolithic landscape by Verve illustrator Kevin Lebon is full of cracked earth, drifting monoliths and fossilised tools. Cave drawings show the age-old frustrations of selling with legacy CRM.

References range from the dawn-of-man opening of the movie 2001: A Space Odyssey (1969) to the ship hovering over the desert in Arrival (2016). Zero’s brand identity sits over the top, sleek and precise, showing how each of those problems gets solved.

Brand character and colour

Verve also created a brand character called Zorb: a gleaming, all-knowing space object with a small dot-matrix face it uses to emote. It makes its moods known through force fields made from hand-drawn cave inscriptions.

Previously, Zero was known for its signature yellow, which came about after the founders originally came up with the startup’s name in a restaurant with yellow tables. Nobody else in the category owns the colour, so Verve decided to keep it on board, pairing it with a deep oxblood and a soft blue, while the typeface is Install by Calame.Bureau.

Craft that scales

Lebon drew the illustrations by hand, then fed them into Figma Weave, an AI tool, to generate large numbers of new landscapes and scenes within the same art direction. That sounds like the sort of thing many agencies are doing with AI these days, but generally like to keep it on the downlow. Walewijn, though, feels he has nothing to hide.

“I’m a little allergic to people defending craft at all costs, as if the old world and the new can’t mix,” he maintains. “You can have a completely crafted system that also scales with AI tools, as long as our input stays in the lead. Off-kilter thinking you can’t replicate, then scaled. That’s the way to go.”

Zero is the first project to come out of Verve’s new duo model, in which a creative director and a strategist lead each client together, from strategy and creative through to account management. Walewijn and Eveline led the work, with Michelle Arrazcaeta also working on strategy.

“Going through an assignment with creative and strategy side by side, even getting stuck in a museum together, creates very human insights that are hard to replicate,” says Walewijn.

The importance of timing

For Zero, the timing matters. It’s currently moving towards a chat-only, “zero-click” interface, the goal its name partly comes from, and Zorb is designed to become the face of the product as that happens.

“It’s a brand that can mature with them,” says Walewijn. “There’s a whole world here for campaigns and events, and as the product becomes a conversation, Zorb can become the face of everything Zero does.”

Before the rebrand, says Niko Salkola, founding designer at Zero, “we felt that the ideas were running in circles: what are we, what do we look like, and how do we differentiate ourselves?

“Verve helped us align that understanding with the founders and the whole team. The story now feels strong and like something we can build on top of. The amount of work Verve put into building the concept was truly inspiring. It is something we never would have been able to do on our own.”

Seven Books That Show What Architecture Tells Us About Storytelling

It was 1976, and as I drove through Marin County, north of San Francisco, an enormous building emerged from the distant hills. It seemed almost otherworldly, as if a spacecraft had landed in a field and burrowed its way into the ground.

It was the Marin County Civic Center, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.

I was captivated by this strange, futuristic building. Its muted pink structure and long, low profile extended into the valley, while its circular and semicircular openings were classical and serene. The building seemed to belong to the landscape even as it challenged it.

I didn’t have the vocabulary then to explain what I was experiencing. I only knew that a structure had altered my perception of the world around it.

Years later, I understood that my draw towards architecture was the relationship between structure and experience. How does a room hold memory? How does a building establish a sense of place? What happens to a structure when people inhabit it, when their histories become entangled with its own?

These questions are not so different from those a writer might ask. A novel, like a building, has a framework (beginning, middle, and end) that holds its parts together: passages that lead us from one place to another, openings that illuminate or obscure a path. Within this framework, writers use language and syntax as an architect uses a straight-edge and pencil. But the most compelling buildings, like the most compelling stories, are more than the sum of their parts. Something happens when human experience enters the structure of both: they’re altered by memory and imagination, capable of holding meanings its creator may never have intended.

When I write, I return to a handful of books that have helped me think about the connections between writing and architecture. Each offers a way of thinking about the relationship between the structures we create and the lives we live within them. And each, in its own way, has something to tell us about storytelling.

*

Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space

A paperback copy of this book was given to me in 1975 by an architect friend. I read it cover to cover and still have that same dog-eared copy, its spine broken, its loose pages held together with tape.

It opened a door for me.

Bachelard writes about the house as a place of reverie and memory. The attic, cellar, drawer, corner, nest—these ordinary spaces become charged with our inner lives. The house is not simply a structure that protects us; it becomes a structure within us.

For writers, Bachelard offers something essential: the understanding that place is never merely a physical backdrop. Rooms can carry emotional history that a character cannot always articulate. The smallest physical detail can be a portal into memory. And often a place we have left behind continues to inhabit us more powerfully than the place in which we presently live.

Bachelard gave me permission to think about architecture lyrically, just as one may think about a poem or prose: the words and the images free our minds up to fall beneath the surface, to tune into the cadence of the subconscious.

Charles Moore, Gerald Allen, and Donlyn Lyndon, The Place of Houses

The premise of The Place of Houses is deceptively simple: to look closely at the ordinary things that make a house feel uniquely one’s own, while understanding the house within the larger context of its community and landscape. A house should not simply look good from the outside. It should feel good to inhabit.

Something similar happens in fiction. A writer imagines not only the world in which a story takes place, but how a character moves through that world. Where does she feel safe, protected, exposed? What does she see from her window? Which room does she avoid? What does she carry from one place to another?

The relationship between inside and outside is especially compelling. A threshold is never simply a doorway. It marks a passage between different kinds of experience, between the intimacy of the private world and the uncertainty of what lies beyond it.

One of the authors, Donlyn Lyndon, once spoke to me about the importance of establishing a sense of place, of allowing the landscape to suggest the patterns from which the building emerges. I remember the conversation about the wild, unprotected outdoors and the shelter of the interior. Neither could be fully understood without the other; in that understanding, he said, lies the balance between outdoors and indoors.

A story, too, establishes its own geography, of both exposure and refuge. The places characters inhabit can reveal the tensions between their inner and outer lives, often more eloquently than anything they say.

Christopher Alexander, A Pattern Language

Christopher Alexander’s A Pattern Language proposes that the places in which we feel most comfortable and alive share recurring patterns. These patterns exist at every scale, from the arrangement of a town to the placement of a window seat. They’re not matters of style or taste: they reflect something elemental about the ways human beings seek comfort, connection, privacy, and belonging. Like spoken and written language, which is made up of simple and complex sentence structures, Alexander’s pattern language offers a vocabulary from which an almost infinite number of combinations can emerge.

Writers also draw upon patterns that give a story its coherence. The intimate language between lovers and friends is different from the language used in public. A gesture repeated at different moments. An object that acquires new meaning each time it appears. A place to which a character returns, changed by what has happened in the intervening years.

Like the patterns Alexander describes, these elements can be deceptively simple. Their power comes from their relationships to one another;…

How Important Were Medieval Viking Drinking Games?

It’s clear from mythology that alcohol was ritually significant in Norse culture, and none more so than mead, which was considered a godly drink and one that imbued the drinker with poetic skill.

In the ancient sagas the origin story of mead comes from a daring series of thefts, with the drink first created through the spit-based peace negotiations of two warring god-families. Their congealing spit, naturally, birthed a mystic with the highest intelligence called Kvasir whose blood was in fact all mead, and through this blood flowed poetry itself.

Unfortunately, Kvasir was not intelligent enough to avoid murder by dwarves for his blood-mead, and then this precious liquid was stolen again by a giant. Odin, king of the gods, wanted his own share of this bloody-mega-mead and so disguised himself as an eagle and stole the mead from the giant, allegedly seducing the giant’s daughter in the process. As Odin escaped from the giant’s lair, some of the mead was spilled from his eagle’s beak and fell to earth. It was said that the great Norse saga poets were those folk who by luck were struck by drops of falling mead from Odin’s beak.

Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty.

*

Beyond the wild and winding escapades of the gods in pursuit of blood-mead, we know a lot of drinking also happened in the mortal Norse realms. Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty and signing contracts, from marriage to inheritance. This drinking, along with most other gatherings (and anything else, for that matter), would take place in the hall, the only place to be in Norse society, what with the winter weather and limited fuel for fires. It was in these halls that the very important business of feast-throwing and drinking in honor of a lord or warrior would take place.

The feast, a sometimes days- or weeks-long exhibition of power and hospitality by the host, was a common (if extraordinarily expensive) way of gift-giving and demon-strating respect among the elites of Norse society. A big bouquet for your sister’s birthday or a nice dessert to take to your aunt’s weekend lunch seems more reasonable now. Great halls designed for this purpose would ring with music, played on bone flutes, bells, stringed instruments and rattles, as well as shields, which were beaten as drums. Such music would be accompanied by other entertainment, including dramatic performances of the old sagas. Drinking was such an integral part of these feasting celebrations that some later sagas show those who did not drink being ostracized from the retinue of their host with some hostility, their lack of involvement seen as an affront.

This binding together of drinkers was done through a (perhaps unhygienic) custom of sumbl, a ritual ceremony also known as “oath cup,” where a woman, often related to the host, would share out a ritual drink among the gathering, one sip at a time and from the same glass. It’s possible women undertook this as a nod to their perceived magical power, and their role as brewers too. The order of those served would help establish the hierarchy of the gathering, a diplomatic tightrope no doubt decided carefully by the hosting household. In the sagas, this drinking ritual was often accompanied by an oath or vow.

In Beowulf, an Anglo-Saxon poem recounting a saga, Queen Wealhtheow is the cupbearer at a sumbl, greeting her husband and king, Horthgar, with drink first before serving others in turn. Beowulf the warrior takes an oath through this ceremony of the bragafull after being challenged by the Queen to rid her hall, the hall of Heorot, of the evil beast that stalks it. Oath-making and -keeping, though, could be lower stakes than defending a hall from its dragon enemies; marriages, alliances and other agreements were kept as oaths, and bound often with communal drinking as a shared witness.

For those not rich, battle-famous or influential enough to be invited to the great feasts in the chieftain’s hall, they too found a way to enjoy a glass or two after a tough day on the fjords. This took place in the Skytningar, a more informal refectory, essentially a pub, where individuals paid their own dues, rather than the quite expensive business of throwing a feast and footing the bill for everyone. As a result, these drinking places attracted the less wealthy looking for a fix, like farmers, merchants and townsfolk. These everyday dives tended to have a pretty bad reputation, the mark of a good time no doubt.

Foreign merchants were often blamed for the noisy impact of these drinking houses on their surroundings, with Snorri’s Olaf’s saga recording how between 1067 and 1093 King Óláfr Haraldsson Kyrri was displeased with the “drinking bouts in marketplaces about the land as a consequence of the large number of merchants.” Later Norwegian kings also continued to rail against the drunkenness of the common man, with King Sverrir in 1300 making a speech against the drunkenness of both his people and the troublesome Germans, who had proved such effective merchants that the stronger wine they traded could now be bought at a price equivalent to local ales, causing outrageous drunkenness among townsfolk.

From gods stealing blood-mead from their giant enemies, to warrior chieftains feasting, toasting and oath making in their great halls, Norse society was intertwined with alcohol.

Heart, the Heretic: The Forgotten Visionary Jane Ellen Harrison on Critical Thinking, Emotional Imagination, and How to Fix the World

By Maria Popova

When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma.

The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in Alpha and Omega (public library) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on the art of growing older, published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

Harrison writes:

The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.

Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in timeless manifesto for freedom of thought, Harrison adds:

The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that “masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,” she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.

[…]

Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.

[…]

We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.…

Kylie Cheung on the Fake Victimhood of Abusers, From Johnny Depp to Israel

In the spring of 2022, Kylie Cheung was reporting for Jezebel on stories she considered urgent; stories about sexual assault and intimate partner violence. In the background, a celebrity defamation trial was being livestreamed on social media. As she watched Johnny Depp’s legal team recast Amber Heard’s resistance to his abuse as proof that she was the abuser, Cheung came to see the trial as a textbook case of DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender—the abuser’s playbook that psychologist Jennifer Freyd named in 1997.

Playing the Victim: How Empires and Abusers Fake Victimhood to Hold Power—And How We Fight Back (North Atlantic Books) follows that playbook from the intimate to the imperial. Cheung argues that powerful institutions, from the Israeli state to anti-abortion lawmakers to the U.S. immigration system, hold on to power by performing victimhood and casting the people they oppress as the aggressors. Israel’s genocide in Gaza is the book’s central case study. Drawing on interviews with human rights lawyers, humanitarian workers, doctors and sexual violence researchers, Cheung documents the sexual and reproductive violence inflicted on Palestinians and the rape atrocity propaganda used to justify it.

Cheung and I spoke about how a celebrity trial became a book about empire, what it means to write about a genocide as it unfolds, and what this work costs the people who do it.

*

Samaa Khullar: The book opens with your 2022 coverage of Depp v. Heard, and you write that it would fundamentally alter your understanding of power and patriarchy. You also said at the book launch that you feel bad about initially viewing the trial as a frivolous thing to be covering. When did that viewpoint change?

Kylie Cheung: As I was following the beginning of the trial in the background, I was frustrated about having to cover what I saw at the time as celebrity news. But the more I saw this huge outpouring of misogyny toward someone who was very obviously a survivor of sexual and domestic violence, the more deeply I started to look into both the case and the strategies being used against this woman who was a survivor.

SK: You do a really great job of showing us the connection between an abuse case like this and the manner in which a modern empire consolidates its power. Can you talk a little bit about that.

KC: For a long time, you would typically think of imperial superpowers as consolidating and maintaining their power through shows of strength. Fascism itself is often rooted in these displays of big, strong men projecting an image of strength. But a lot of them actually consolidate and maintain their power by playing victim, by performing some amount of victimhood. The people they are oppressing, the population they’re holding captive or occupying or abusing, they portray as this giant, towering, bestial oppressor. And that then justifies the horrific violence that they enact.

With the Johnny Depp and Amber Heard case, his team really tried to float this idea of mutual abuse. They weren’t really even denying that he had been violent toward her. They were just trying to frame it as: “She was violent, too, in all of these different ways.” Confusing everyone and pretending that they were both equally violent toward each other was so effective because there’s this vast public illiteracy about the dynamics of domestic abuse and the tactics of domestic abusers, not to mention the nature of power dynamics. Nowhere have I seen that more starkly than in Israel’s genocide in Palestine.

There are so many things in this book, especially where Israel and Palestine are concerned, that could have been written before 2023.

SK: How do you write a book about a moving target? When do you decide you have to stop and contextualize it at this moment? There’s always going to be the next story and the next story. For an article or a newspaper, you’re able to trace that, but it’s different with a book like this.

KC: I did have to be conscientious while writing, and get grounded in the context of where I was writing it from. As I talked about a bit at the book launch, this has been true of my work on abortion bans and sexual violence and the carceral system: It can feel like this itch in your brain where you want to have as many examples as possible. Fundamentally, though, you find that the thesis, the main points of critique, don’t really change. There are so many things in this book, especially where Israel and Palestine are concerned, that could have been written before 2023. It’s the same tactics of genocide and occupation.

A few months ago, the Palestinian Feminist Collective put out this really powerful and important report documenting how systematic the sexual violence that Israel is perpetrating is. I really wish I could have included that in the book. But at the same time, all of that vitally important and devastating data builds on what we have all long known, which is that Israel is carrying out this mass state-sanctioned sexual violence against Palestinians.

SK: I also want to ask about what didn’t make the book. A lot of people are probably expecting you to talk about the Cornell rape case—the details of which came out after the book went to print. It feels very relevant to your arguments in the book, especially as more of Jane Doe’s alleged assaulters come out and say, “Well, actually, she initiated this,” or “If you look at our texts afterward, she was apologizing to us, and now she’s flipping the script!” Had this lawsuit gone public before publishing, where do you think it would fit in the book’s framework?…

8 Retellings of Classics That Put BIPOC Writers at the Center

Below, she recommends eight retellings of classics by BIPOC authors. (Photo credit: Frank W Images.)

Clueless is the reason I read Emma. I was a teenager who could recite Cher Horowitz’s one-liners from memory. When I want to hurt someone’s feelings, I just call them a virgin who can’t drive. When somebody told me a white woman in a bonnet had written the original, I went to get into white folks’ business immediately.

I’m a cultural anthropologist by training, and reading Austen felt like fieldwork. She studied families, who can marry whom, who inherits the house, whose bad decision drags down prospects. Anyone raised around aunties, church mothers, a family group chat with cousins in three time zones, or a grandmother who can place a boy’s people from his last name already knows how that system works. Plenty of us didn’t need Regency England to learn that a marriage is a negotiation between families. We learned it at the cookout, at the masjid, at the wedding where somebody’s mother asked what your father does before she asked your name.

Jane Austen’s Regency concerns have traveled exceptionally well.

For many BIPOC communities, those same concerns have additional histories of migration, colonialism, racial exclusion, and economic precarity. There is also just something delicious about writers of color getting their hands on the Western literary canon. These are stories that have been presented to us as universal, even when their imagined worlds rarely made room for people who looked like us. And yet, we’ve found ourselves in them anyway.

The following eight novels take familiar stories and give them new cultural, political, and emotional dimensions. Most are affectionate reinterpretations of Austen. Others have legitimate grievances with the source material. All of them demonstrate how much literary possibility exists when writers are allowed to bring their entire histories to the page.

Pride and Protest by Nikki Payne, inspired by Pride and Prejudice

My own book! Liza B. is “the only DJ who gives a Jam”. She’s fighting to save Longbourne Gardens, the low-income complex in her DC neighborhood that Pemberley Development wants to replace with luxury condos and high-end pet spas. At the company’s gala, she stages a flash protest and mistakes its acting CEO, Dorsey Fitzgerald, for one of the waitstaff. Dorsey is a Filipino heir adopted into the family business and still trying to prove he deserves it, which makes his pride a lot more anxious than the original’s. Liza’s prejudices, meanwhile, are mostly correct. A snowstorm that traps them in the Pemberley offices handles the rest.

Unmarriageable by Soniah Kamal, inspired by Pride and Prejudice

Kamal rewrites Austen’s most famous first sentence on page one and then moves the whole Bennet operation to the fictional town of Dilwale, Pakistan. Alys Binat teaches English literature at a girls’ school and keeps telling her students that marriage is a choice, which would be easier to say if her family hadn’t lost its money and her mother didn’t have five daughters to place. What Kamal understands is that Mrs. Bennet was never a joke. She’s a woman doing crisis management in a culture where a daughter’s marriage doubles as the family’s retirement plan. The best scenes are Alys teaching Pride and Prejudice to girls who already know the plot from their own living rooms.

Ayesha at Last by Uzma Jalaluddin, inspired by Pride and Prejudice

Ayesha Shamsi wants to be a poet. For now she’s a substitute teacher in Toronto, living with a grandfather who quotes Shakespeare at dinner and a younger cousin, Hafsa, who collects marriage proposals like trading cards. Then comes Khalid Mirza, with his beard and his white robes and his judgments, and the two of them are thrown together planning a conference at the mosque. Jalaluddin splits the pride and the prejudice between them so nobody gets to be the only fool. She also lets their faith stay in the room the entire time. Nobody has to give it up to earn the happy ending, and that is rarer in romance than it ought to be.

Pride by Ibi Zoboi, inspired by Pride and Prejudice

In this YA novel, Zoboi turns the Bennets into the Benitez sisters, five Afro-Latina girls of Haitian and Dominican descent living in a Bushwick walk-up while the block changes around them faster than the rent. When the wealthy Darcys move into the renovated house across the street, Zuri Benitez decides she hates their son Darius before he opens his mouth, mostly because of what his family’s money means for everyone else on the block. Zuri writes poetry and has strong opinions about who belongs in Bushwick, and Zoboi takes both seriously.

Escaping Mr. Rochester by L.L. McKinney, inspired by Jane Eyre

Every reader of Jane Eyre eventually has to reckon with the woman in the attic. Jean Rhys started that argument in 1966. McKinney settles it by letting Bertha Mason speak for herself. In this YA remix, Jane and Bertha are both Black, Bertha is from New Orleans, and Rochester has locked her away for refusing to hand over her inheritance. How to Bear Your Desolations

The morning after a relationship of depth and significance long bending under the weight of its own complexity had finally broken with an exhausted thud, I opened the kiln to discover a month’s worth of pottery shattered — two pieces had exploded, the shrapnel ruining the rest. All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy.

And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open.

Breaking alive.

It is not an easy assignment, being alive. Coming awake from the stupor of near-living that lulls us through our days, awake to the knowledge that on the other side of the neighborhood ICE trucks are handcuffing people and on the other side of the planet children are dying in gunfire, while outside the first birds of spring are singing and everywhere people are falling in love and in some faraway mountain village a shepherd is singing under a thousand stars. And somehow, somehow, all of it has to cohere into a single world in which we, in all our incohesion, must live this single life.

Ellen Bass reckons with all of this in her splendid poem “Any Common Desolation,” originally published in The Academy of American Poets’ poem-a-day newsletter and later included in James Crews’s lifeline of an anthology How to Love the World: Poems of Gratitude and Hope (public library), shared here with Ellen’s blessing.

ANY COMMON DESOLATION

by Ellen Bass

can be enough to make you look up

at the yellowed leaves of the apple tree, the few

that survived the rains and frost, shot

with late afternoon sun. They glow a deep

orange-gold against a blue so sheer, a single bird

would rip it like silk. You may have to break

your heart, but it isn’t nothing

to know even one moment alive. The sound

of an oar in an oarlock or a ruminant

animal tearing grass. The smell of grated ginger.

The ruby neon of the liquor store sign.

Warm socks. You remember your mother,

her precision a ceremony, as she gathered

the white cotton, slipped it over your toes,

drew up the heel, turned the cuff. A breath

can uncoil as you walk across your own muddy yard,

the big dipper pouring night down over you, and everything

you dread, all you can’t bear, dissolves

and, like a needle slipped into your vein —

that sudden rush of the world.

Complement with Henry James on how to stop waiting and start living and Hermann Hesse on how to be more alive, then revisit Ellen’s magnificent poem “How to Apologize.” And if you are looking to break your poetry open, I couldn’t recommend her Living Room Craft Talks more heartily.

Ruth

There is the house in the town where Ruth grew up and ran away from. There is the door with the lock and the garden with the tree and the school car park in the darkness. There is the river hurrying out of the town and passing through the country and to the sea. There is Ruth when she was a child and the dream of the island moved up the walls of her room and became almost all she could see. There is, now, Ruth—a decade gone from the house in the town—on the island, finally. There is the island. Here it is. Magnificent and terrifying, divine. It was made so long ago, it was battered by ice from the rock. Here and there, in the craggy cliff, the ground opens up, smaller and larger entrances leading to caves and tunnels below, the gush and bellow of the sea moving in and out. At the highest point, a white exclamation mark: a lighthouse.

Ruth leaves her daughter at the lighthouse and walks out to the cliff. At some point she stops and looks back to see if she can make out the clearing where Ori waits, but already it is out of sight. She keeps going. She sees birds with white-tipped arrow wings, seals slipping into the water. She sees beaches protected from the wind. She must go back now. She must. OK, she says, here I come.

She turns and starts walking back to Ori. The ground is treacherous. The island spins around her, fills her; she keeps walking. As she walks she gives away some of the island—it belongs only to her, beloved, the clear and ringing dream of it that she has had since she was a child in that house by the river—and she thinks: I am walking to Ori. I am walking back to Ori. They will return to the caravan now, to JP and Nora and Leo. She walks fast. She will take her daughter back to real life now and save them both from the tangles of this swooping dream. She walks, thinking of the words she will say to Ori. I love you, I will always love you. The ground ahead is—

Ori

Along the paper fold of the country, there is an island. The cliff winds are hard and wild but the derelict, long‑abandoned lighthouse is in a clearing surrounded by scrubby trees. The doorway of the lighthouse is a mouth,

the concrete floor inside is cracked open, weed‑covered.

In the clearing Ori waits for her mother to come back. The stones she has found here are so, so beautiful. Grey with darker bands, others mottled and rough, a few with holes bored right through them. She strokes them against her cheeks, puts them in her mouth, fills her pockets. She is six years old and wearing red dungarees and torn bee wings, she is singing songs without words into the tickling wind, she is waiting for her mother to come back to her. They will go home, they will eat Chinese takeaway, they will tell the others about their trip, the island will be a story again. This is what will happen.

*

It begins to get dark. She crawls into the sleeping bag and pulls it shut over her head. When she hears her mother coming, she will wait and wait and then she will leap out. SURPRISE!

When she wakes her mother has still not returned. Ori is wrapped in the sleeping bag, underneath the sky. She gets on all fours and looks around. She needs a wee. She needs something to drink. She is hungry. She stands and shouts her mother’s name. She shouts and shouts and shouts until her throat is sore. She retreats inside the lighthouse. She wets herself, as she has not done for a long time, and it is warm until it cools uncomfortably. She calls for Ruth. She calls her by every name she has ever called her by. She gets out of the sleeping bag and drinks water from the little spring with her hands. She gets a Babybel from the bag and eats it.

She dozes in the doorway of the lighthouse. When she wakes there is a ghost dancing. It is a hare. She screams for Ruth and the hare does not run but freezes, flattened on its belly, waiting.

Night, and a dark so impenetrable she cannot even see the tree two paces in front of her. She pulls the sleeping bag over her head.

*

A storm comes. Rain first and then thunder, getting closer. She is afraid and hides inside the lighthouse. The storm is directly overhead. Momentous clashes of sound, the rain spattering through holes in the ceiling, the lightning illuminating the jaggedy branches of the trees.

When she wakes, she understands immediately her mistake. The storm has blown itself out and the sky is white and gentle. She fumbles out of the sleeping bag, kicking it aside. She takes out two smooth stones from her pocket and holds them in her hands. There is the smell, still, of the burnt brambles, the charred walls. She holds one stone in each hand and knocks and knocks them together. Surely the sound must travel across the whole island. And yes, there, someone is coming into the clearing. Her mother is coming through the trees towards her.

She thinks that the sky is filling with pieces of cut paper, like snow; although it is not. White particles turn into flakes turn into sheets until everything is blank.

Min

It is March, the spring equinox. The man named Min is on the island to look for hares. He has pitched his tent

in the island lowlands. There are traces of the hares everywhere, although for two days he does not see them. The distinctive, long footprints run circles around him; on the rock he finds their droppings and in the grass signs of abandoned forms. A few times, carried on the wind, he thinks he hears their warning thumps, although he cannot be certain. An enclosed environment like the island could be the perfect place for his experiment. He finds himself easily tired, out of breath even after a small walk or climb. He thinks that he must dream in the tent. He is studying the dreams of hares and surely he must also dream.…

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In all the Universe, there’s no bigger question — and no greater mystery — than where all of this came from, and how all of this came to be. For countless generations, our cosmic origins were a question for poets, theologians, and philosophers, as our scientific knowledge had not yet advanced to the point where we could uncover an evidence-based answer to such questions. However, the 20th and 21st centuries changed all of that, allowing us to pin down the answers to such questions as:

- What rules govern our Universe?

- What is the Universe made of?

- How large and how old is it?

- How did it come to be the way it is today?

- And what are our ultimate cosmic origins?

We often say, now, that our Universe began with the hot Big Bang, but that’s only the Universe as we know and experience it today: the observable Universe. We’ve since learned that the Big Bang itself was preceded and set up by an earlier phase in cosmic history: cosmic inflation, where space itself contained an enormous amount of inherent energy and expanded — or inflated — rapidly and relentlessly. When inflation ended, our hot Big Bang ensued, giving rise to the Universe as we know, observe, and exist within it.

But what, exactly, were inflation’s properties? What type of inflation occurred, and what relics, or imprints, of inflation remain within our observable Universe today? Although we’ve come remarkably far in our understanding of our cosmic origins, there are a few windows still left unexplored that can take our understanding to the next level. Here are the three big ones where new data will help guide the way.

We truly went from not knowing what the Universe was, at all, to figuring out an enormous about about our cosmic origins in the span of less than 150 years. Our journey began in earnest in the late 19th century, when people began to notice breakdowns in Newtonian mechanics at speeds close to the speed of light, and hints of a breakdown in Newtonian gravity when it came to the orbit of the planet Mercury. Both of those puzzles were eventually resolved with Einstein and relativity: special relativity for Newtonian mechanics, and general relativity, incorporating gravity in a relativistic framework, to eventually resolve the precession of Mercury’s perihelion.

Within that new framework for gravity, several new exact solutions emerged. These included the:

- Minkowski solution, which reduces to flat, uncurved, matter-free space,

- Schwarzschild solution, for a non-rotating black hole,

- de Sitter solution, for a Universe dominated by a cosmological constant, and

- Friedmann solution, for a Universe that was both isotropic (the same in all directions) and homogeneous (the same in all locations) and filled evenly with at least one form of energy.

Friedmann’s solution, derived in 1922, was particularly interesting from a cosmic perspective, because it showed that static spacetimes that were uniformly filled with “stuff” were unstable; the Universe must expand or contract.

Contemporaneously, starting in 1923, we began identifying individual stars within the spiral and elliptical nebulae in the skies: determining that they were galaxies beyond the Milky Way. When we combined those distance measurements with redshift measurements, or how fast these galaxies appeared to recede from us, we found a relationship: the farther the galaxy, the faster the recession speed. When this relationship was placed into the context of Friedmann’s solution, we arrived at the expanding Universe: the first big step towards understanding our cosmic origins.

Grateful for curious minds

If the Universe is expanding today, then that means things are getting farther apart, becoming less dense, and — since the wavelength of radiation is stretching to become longer — cooling as well. If things are getting less dense and cooling today, that means that they were denser and hotter in the past. Since gravitation attracts objects and brings them together, the Universe should become more structure rich, i.e., clumpier, as time goes on as well. Therefore, this points towards an early state of the Universe that was hotter, denser, and more uniform than it is today.

If you start off with a very hot, very dense, very uniform, and rapidly expanding Universe, then as time goes on, the following sets of things will occur.

- Particles will clump together, forming protons and neutrons, and then protons and neutrons will fuse together into atomic nuclei: creating an initial set of elements even before stars have formed.

- Atomic nuclei and electrons will combine together, and as the Universe cools sufficiently to make stable, neutral atoms, any photons (or radiation) that was present back then will simply stream outward in a straight line, stretching in wavelength and cooling as the Universe expands to create a persistent background of radiation: the CMB.

- Gravitation will pull matter together into clumps: creating stars, star clusters, small galaxies, larger galaxies, groups and clusters of galaxies, and even grander structures akin to a cosmic web. As time goes on, this web-like structure gets more well-defined and more pronounced.

- And the Universe keeps on expanding, with the expansion rate changing as the density of the Universe changes, resulting in a particular relationship between the expansion rate over time and the matter-and-energy contents of the Universe.

These are the four cornerstones of the hot Big Bang, and all four have been observationally confirmed.…

Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They’re entirely undeterred by the radiation – in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

The same type of species, Cladosporium sphaerospermum, has grown on the International Space Station, about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above the surface of the Earth, in an experiment to test its resistance to radiation. Scientists found that it appeared to block a small amount of incoming radiation, and part of why comes down to a pigment called melanin.

I used to think of melanin the way most people do – as a pigment that gives skin, hair and eyes their color. That changed early in my Ph.D. research when I read a 2019 study from the materials science lab I was joining that described how to make a fungal form of melanin in the lab. I was surprised by where this pigment shows up in nature, including in fungi growing at Chernobyl.

Melanin comprises a family of pigments. The melanin in human skin, called eumelanin, is built from nitrogen-containing building blocks. The melanin in many fungi, called allomelanin, is built from a different, nitrogen-free building block. That difference in structure gives it some unusual properties.

Scientists think allomelanin is a large part of why these fungi can live in such places. Over the course of my doctoral research, I learned that melanin does much more than add color. It holds onto metals, absorbs ultraviolet light, converts light into heat and helps produce the colors of some bird feathers.

Allomelanin has another remarkable property. My colleagues showed in 2021 that lab-made allomelanin is full of built-in pores, each less than a billionth of a meter wide. Chemists call these pores “intrinsic pores” because they are part of the material’s natural structure, rather than etched in later. To our knowledge, it is the only type of melanin with built-in porosity.

These nanometer-wide pores let the pigment act like a sponge for small molecules, including toxic ones, a feature we confirmed holds true whether the allomelanin comes directly from natural fungi or whether it is synthesized in our lab.

In a recent study published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal ACS Nano, my colleagues and I asked whether this material could do more than trap toxic chemicals. Could it also break them down?

Chemistry behind nerve agents and pesticides

Nerve agents such as sarin and VX belong to a group of chemicals called organophosphorus compounds. They block an enzyme the body uses to switch off nerve signals. Without that enzyme, nerves keep firing continuously, and a large enough exposure can turn lethal within minutes.

Chemical weapons are banned under international law, but they remain a persistent security concern. In May 2026, inspectors from the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons reported discovering dozens of previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria left over from the Assad government.

Many pesticides used on agricultural crops rely on this exact same underlying chemistry. A 2026 analysis estimated that accidental pesticide poisonings number in the hundreds of millions each year, resulting in roughly 11,000 deaths annually around the world. Farmworkers operating with minimal protective gear face the greatest ongoing risk.

Today’s protective suits mostly rely on materials like activated carbon, which trap the chemicals but don’t break them down. Soldiers and farmworkers could benefit from protective gear that does more than block these toxic chemicals. Researchers, including my colleagues, are working on materials that could neutralize them as well.

Adding a catalyst: Turning a sponge into scissors

Allomelanin on its own holds on to these organophosphorus molecules but leaves them chemically intact. A contaminated glove or mask that has merely trapped these toxins would remain hazardous to handle.

To improve our sponge, my colleagues and I made allomelanin in the form of tiny spheres, each hundreds of times narrower than a human hair. We then added tiny clusters made of a metal called zirconium. Each cluster consists of six zirconium atoms anchored by oxygen – it looks like a tiny cage of zirconium held together by oxygen.

Similar zirconium clusters form the active core of metal-organic frameworks, which are among the most studied materials for degrading chemical weapons. These clusters act like molecular scissors: When exposed to ambient moisture, they snip the chemical bonds holding organophosphates together, splitting them into less harmful pieces.

We tested different ways to attach these metal clusters to our synthetic allomelanin particles, ensuring the molecular scissors sat right where incoming toxins would land.

For safety, we tested the particles with a chemical stand-in widely used in research laboratories. It mimics nerve agents but carries far less toxicity. Our best-performing versions broke down half of the target chemical in less than 10 minutes, using only a tiny amount of zirconium. The particles kept working over several rounds of use, with very little metal leaking out.

Allomelanin’s built-in pores turned out to be essential. When we added the same zirconium clusters to other melanin-like materials without pores, they barely facilitated the breakdown. Adding too much zirconium also slowed the reaction, likely because more clusters clogged up the pores that water and toxic molecules needed to travel through. The best results came from balancing the amount of metal with open pore space.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The sold-out crowd at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium, better known as “The Swamp,” roared with excitement as the University of Florida revived its “Gator bait” cheer at its 2026 season opener.

When the marching band played the familiar cue, thousands of fans responded with the “Gator chomp,” raising their outstretched arms and repeatedly opening and closing their hands like alligator jaws while shouting “Gator bait!”

The decision to bring back the popular cheer reversed a ban imposed in 2020 by University of Florida President Kent Fuchs, who was concerned about its racist origins amid the nationwide reckoning over race that followed the murder of George Floyd.

Current university president Stuart Bell remarked in an interview prior to his official appointment that “traditions matter” and suggested that the cheer could return because it remained “meaningful to the Gator family.” Since then, the university has restored the cheer, though it has not publicly identified who formally authorized its return.

The controversy surrounding this chant has often been framed narrowly by its supporters as a dispute over tradition versus political correctness. However, it raises important questions about whether a public university should continue to embrace a tradition that risks making some students and alumni feel less welcome on campus.

As an environmental and cultural historian and author of “Gator!: The Making of America’s Iconic Reptile, from First Encounters to Florida Man,” I’ve spent years researching how alligators became intertwined with ideas about race, nature and Southern identity. My research points to a deeper history largely absent from the public debate over the cheer.

The making of ‘alligator bait’ as a racial slur

The roots of the “alligator bait” trope stretch back to the 18th century, when French explorers in North America claimed that a “certain exhalation” given off from Black skin attracted the voracious reptiles.

White plantation owners eagerly took up this racist theory because it discouraged enslaved people from fleeing into Southern swamps and marshes, where pursuing runaways was often difficult.

After the Civil War, as formerly enslaved people sought economic, educational and political advancement, many white Americans responded with efforts to reassert white supremacy. Alongside disenfranchisement, Jim Crow segregation and racial terrorism, they promoted stereotypes that demeaned and dehumanized African Americans.

One of these racist stereotypes was the depiction of Black Americans, especially children, as natural prey for alligators. Though it operated through images and ideas rather than physical force, the stereotype reinforced beliefs in Black inferiority. It also helped justify the intimidation, exclusion and violence that African Americans routinely faced during this period.

It was in this context that the racial slur “alligator bait” began circulating widely in the late 19th century. A bestselling photograph bearing that title, published in 1897, helped popularize the slur. Although the composite image of nine naked African American toddlers did not include an actual alligator, its title invited viewers to imagine Black children as special targets of the reptile.

The epithet soon spread through newspapers, postcards, editorial cartoons, songs and films. Ostensibly humorous images of alligators threatening or consuming Black Americans, especially children, also circulated widely across the U.S.

Whether Black children were ever actually used as bait to hunt alligators remains a subject of historical debate. But what is beyond dispute is that these images helped entrench degrading associations between African Americans and alligators in American popular culture for decades.

‘Gator bait’ comes to campus

As the phrase alligator bait gained currency across the United States, it also began appearing in a new setting: University of Florida football games. The earliest published reference to the cheer seems to be a 1939 newspaper account of a home game against Georgia Tech.

When Georgia Tech’s Yellow Jackets took the field, Florida students taunted the all-white team with cries of “alligator bait.” Georgia Tech’s coach used the insult to motivate his players, asking whether they could imagine “anything lower than that.”

While it is impossible to know precisely how everyone present understood the phrase, it entered Florida football culture at a time when “alligator bait” remained a recognizable racial slur. By the late 1940s, the shortened form, “Gator bait,” which was both easier to chant and more closely aligned with the university’s “Gators” nickname, had become a regular fixture at Florida football games.

The cheer remained firmly embedded in campus culture as the university navigated the slow and often contentious process of desegregation. Like most Southern universities, the University of Florida resisted admitting Black students, enrolling its first African American law student, George H. Starke, only after a court order in 1958. The first Black undergraduates arrived four years later, and the football team remained segregated until 1968.

Desegregation did not immediately transform the broader campus culture. The university continued to embrace traditions that celebrated the Confederacy and romanticized the Old South. In 1962, football coach Ray Graves placed decals of the Confederate battle flag on his players’ helmets before the Gator Bowl.

As late as the 1970s, the all-white Kappa Alpha fraternity continued a decades-long tradition of staging an annual “Old South” weekend that featured students parading in Confederate uniforms. In the 1950s and 1960s, that celebration even included a mock execution of Union General William T. Sherman and a secession proclamation.…

item.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Roughly half of the world’s population speaks more than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.

Throughout history, various people have attracted attention for their remarkable linguistic abilities. Some have genuinely mastered numerous languages, while others have exaggerated their proficiency or struggled to demonstrate their purported abilities.

In my 2026 book “Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language,” I explore the science of language, including how people acquire, understand and use it, from childhood language development to learning additional languages.

The word polyglot comes from the Greek word polyglōttos, meaning “many-tongued.” It describes someone who speaks multiple languages, but it leaves some important questions unanswered: How many languages must someone know, and how proficient must they be, to earn the title?

Polyglots throughout time

In the 1998 edition of the “Guinness Book of World Records,” Ziad Youssef Fazah was named the world’s greatest living polyglot. Born in Liberia and raised speaking Arabic, Fazah claimed to speak, read and understand an astonishing 59 languages. At the time, The Washington Post dubbed him the “One-man Tower of Babel.”

He was hardly the first person to attract attention for his supposed extraordinary linguistic abilities.

Cardinal Giuseppe Mezzofanti, an Italian scholar born in 1774, was reportedly proficient in 38 languages.

The 10th-century philosopher Al-Farabi was said to know 70 languages, while the 19th-century German linguist Hans Conon von der Gabelentz was believed to know 80 languages, according to accounts of his linguistic abilities. Sir John Bowring, a British diplomat and governor of Hong Kong, may have known as many as 200 languages.

Such claims are difficult to verify, particularly when they concern historical figures. What counted as knowing a language? Was it familiarity with its vocabulary and grammar, the ability to read and write it, to translate, or to communicate comfortably with native speakers? These are very different levels of linguistic ability.

Fazah’s abilities were put to the test in 1997 on Chilean television. During a live appearance, he was asked basic questions in several languages, including Russian, Greek and Hindi. He struggled to answer correctly, even when asked relatively simple questions. The performance cast serious doubt on his claims, and his name subsequently disappeared from the “Guinness Book of World Records.”

The episode illustrates a crucial distinction: Knowing some of a language is not the same as being fluent in it.

What does it mean to speak a language?

So, how fluent is fluent?

Fluency in a language is not an all-or-nothing achievement. It is a spectrum, ranging from basic conversational ability to sophisticated, near-native command. Someone might understand a language quite well but struggle to speak it. Another person might hold a conversation comfortably but have difficulty reading or writing. Proficiency can vary across the different ways people understand and use a language.

Linguists generally assess language proficiency across several areas, including speaking, listening, reading and writing. These abilities do not necessarily develop at the same rate. A person who can introduce themselves, order a meal and ask for directions may have a useful working knowledge of a language, but that is not the same as being able to debate politics, understand wordplay or conduct professional business in it.

This makes claims about polyglotism particularly difficult to evaluate. There is no simple threshold that determines when someone can legitimately say they speak a language. And counting languages tells us little without knowing the level of proficiency in each.

A genuine linguistic savant

Not all extraordinary claims are exaggerated.

One remarkable example is Christopher Taylor. A British savant who was born in 1960 and died in 2020, Taylor and his language abilities have long been studied by researchers. Savant syndrome is a rare condition in which someone with a developmental or intellectual disability displays exceptional ability in a particular area, such as music, mathematics or, in Taylor’s case, languages.

Taylor experienced significant developmental delays as a child. As an adult he still required support with everyday activities. Yet he demonstrated an extraordinary capacity for learning languages. He could read, write, translate and converse in 15 to 20 languages, including Danish, Dutch, Finnish, German, Greek, Hindi, Italian, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish and Welsh.

His proficiency varied. In some languages he could hold a conversation; in others his understanding was more basic. But his ability to acquire new linguistic knowledge was remarkable. Much of his learning was self-directed, using introductory language books, dictionaries and interactions with native speakers.

In one experiment, published in 1993, Taylor learned the North African language Berber. Researchers found that he quickly grasped aspects of its complex grammar, including patterns of word order and verb agreement. He also mastered an artificial language called Epun, which researchers had invented specifically for the study. This suggested that his abilities extended beyond memorizing familiar words or phrases.

Taylor’s case is extraordinary, but it also offers a useful reminder: Even exceptional language ability comes in degrees. Researchers found that his proficiency varied considerably across languages. He was fluent in some, while in others he had only a basic knowledge. Being able to demonstrate knowledge of a language in a controlled experiment is not necessarily the same as using it fluently in everyday life.

How many languages can someone really learn?

Since the mid-1920s, department store giant Macyâs has held an annual Thanksgiving Day Parade to ring in the holiday shopping season. While many of the paradeâs beloved traditions have remained, the celebration has made some pretty big changes over the course of the last 100 years.

It Was Originally a Christmas Parade

While the parade has by now solidified itself as a Thanksgiving staple across the United States, the extravaganza was originally designed to be a Christmas celebration. When Macyâs first envisioned the parade, it was intended to be a celebration of Christmas staged on Thanksgiving morning to kickoff the holiday shopping season.Â

After the parade debuted in 1924 to celebrate the opening of their flagship store in Herald Square, Macyâs decided to continue the tradition annually, later changing the name from the Macyâs Christmas Parade to the Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade.Â

Early Parades Featured Live Animals

When the parade first debuted in 1924, Macyâs borrowed live animals from the Central Park Zoo for the occasion. Elephants, lions, tigers, bears, and even camels marched the six mile route from Harlem to Macyâs in Herald Square alongside clowns, marching bands, and Santa Claus himself.Â

Macyâs continued featuring live animals in their parade for a few years afterward, but eventually phased them out of the line up when the well-known balloons became the main attraction.Â Â

The Balloons Werenât Always Filled With HeliumÂ

When Macyâs tasked puppeteer Tony Sarg with designing some of their very first balloons, the giant balloons were filled with air instead of helium, requiring them to be propped up by poles instead of floating on their own. By 1928, helium had become more widely commercially available and the balloons were filled with the lightweight gas instead.

During those first few years, the balloons were released into the sky at the end of the parade, but the practice was stopped after a pilot chasing after one nearly crashed.Â

Itâs Taken a Few Years Off

In the more than 100 years Macyâs has held its annual parade, the retail giant has only taken a few years off between 1942 and 1944 on account of the United Statesâ ongoing participation in World War II. Being that rubber and helium were tightly rationed to support the war effort, Macyâs decided to forgo its annual parade in the early 1940s and instead donated rubber from their retired balloons to the U.S. military.Â

By 1945, the war had officially ended and the Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade returned.Â

The Pandemic Changed Things

In November 2020, Macyâs held a scaled back, COVID-conscious iteration of their Thanksgiving Day Parade. Instead of their usual two and a half mile route through Manhattan, the parade festivities all took place just outside Macyâs Herald Square location with a significantly reduced crowd and streaming to audiences quarantining at home.

Alongside pre-taped musical performances, the paradeâs balloons were pulled by specially outfitted vehicles instead of the customary team of handlers. Thankfully, by 2021, the parade was back to its normal standard of spectacle.Â

item.description:

This piece was featured in Issue 25 of Works in Progress.

In 1983, a biochemical company called AGS filed an application to release genetically modified organisms into the environment. AGS had deleted a single gene from a common leaf-dwelling microbe that encoded a protein around which ice crystals nucleate. By removing it and spraying the modified microbes onto plants, AGS hoped to prevent ice from forming on crops during cold California mornings.

At the time, there was no dedicated regulatory process for engineered microbes, so applications defaulted to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), which had laid out voluntary rules and approved AGS’s request to run field trials. But an activist named Jeremy Rifkin then sued to stop the experiments, arguing that the NIH had skipped a required Environmental Impact Statement and that the engineered microbes could scatter into the wild with ‘possible effects on rainfall’. AGS eventually won the right to begin trials on strawberry plants in California in 1987, only for a group of activists to cut through the chain-link fence around the field and uproot about 2,000 of the 2,400 plants.

Rifkin’s lawsuit forced the question of how engineered microbes should be regulated. After the court case, staff at the White House gathered lawyers and regulators from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) to figure out how to handle engineered microbes moving forward. They concluded that no new laws were needed: the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), written in 1976 for industrial chemicals, would apply to engineered microbes as well. These civil servants essentially decided that since genomes are made of chemicals, and novel chemicals are already regulated under the TSCA, engineered microbes with modified genomes were likewise covered.

Since that decision, development of microbes covered by the law has frozen. The TSCA is a regulatory black hole: between 1987 and 2018, researchers filed more than 240 applications. Only a few were ever approved for widespread use.

The world has produced all kinds of marvelous microbes in the last forty years. Genetically engineered microorganisms, for example, can pull nitrogen from the air and detect buried landmines by releasing gases visible to satellites. But almost none have been used, thanks to an American law never meant to regulate biology.

Microbes in limbo

In 2016, Japanese researchers discovered a microbe, Ideonella sakaiensis, growing near a recycling plant. That microbe is able to digest PET, the plastic in water bottles and most polyester clothing. Though technically recyclable, PET must first be shredded, melted, and remolded into new forms, so most just accumulates in landfill.

These wild microbes took an existing protein that degrades cutin (the waxy material on plant leaves) and evolved it to eat plastic instead. But natural forms of the PET-eating enzymes are slow; when the microbes were cultured on top of a thin PET film and incubated at 30 degrees centigrade, it took them six weeks to break it down.

Engineers at the University of Texas at Austin therefore took these PET-eating enzymes and used computational tools to make an improved variant, called FAST-PETase. This enzyme is 98 percent identical to the natural version but digests PET plastics in less than 24 hours. The next step could be to place FAST-PETase back into living cells and release them onto landfills. But even putting the gene back into its original host, I. sakaiensis, triggers TSCA, ensuring that the reconstituted organism can’t be used.

Engineered microbes could also be employed to detect heavy metals in streams and rivers at low concentrations far more cheaply than existing methods. Researchers have already created E. coli that can detect as little as five parts per billion of cadmium ions. In 2010, Chinese students engineered E. coli cells to sense mercury ions in water down to a seven-nanomolar concentration, seven times lower than the EPA’s contamination threshold. But none of these strains can be used outside the lab as all contain intergeneric DNA sequences, meaning they fall under TSCA.

Mining is another missed opportunity. Most metal in ore is discarded, because purification processes generally extract only a single target metal, rather than several at once. The US has enough active mines to meet all of its domestic mineral needs if it could capture 90 percent of the remaining byproducts in the ore. Yet when recovery does happen, it is energy-intensive and usually involves harsh chemicals that release toxic gases.

Bioleaching, a process that uses microbes to recover metals, might be a better option. This is typically done by employing microbes to oxidize iron and sulfur in sulfide ores, kicking off a chain reaction that dissolves out the copper. The same reactions happen without microbes, just too slowly to be industrially useful. Microbes are self-powering and could do the job without making toxic byproducts.

To make bioleaching more efficient, researchers turned to Gluconobacter oxydans B58, a microbe that converts sugars into mineral-dissolving acids. In a 2021 study, Cornell researchers found that 89 genes are involved in making these acids and that, by deleting some while overexpressing others, they could make a variant that extracts rare earth metals 73 percent faster than the ordinary microbe. Those changes didn’t cross genus lines, but even this kind of workaround is frowned upon because deleting a particular gene in a microbe requires introducing a marker, typically an antibiotic resistance gene from another organism, that allows only engineered cells to survive when exposed to antibiotics. As this gene comes from a different organism, adding it can trigger TSCA all by itself.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

In the early hours of 5th June 1967, Gamal ‘Abd al-Nasser, the revolutionary leader of Egypt, received good news from his commanders. The Egyptian Air Force had destroyed three quarters of the Israeli Air Force and was laying waste to what was left of the enemy’s airbases. This information was immediately telegraphed to Egypt’s allies – Syria, Jordan, and Iraq – who enthusiastically entered the fray, expecting a walkover.

Nasser’s commanders hadn’t been entirely honest. Three quarters of an air force had been destroyed, but it was the Egyptian one: the Israelis had bombed 298 of Egypt’s 420 combat aircraft on the tarmac. In the face of the lightning Israeli ground offensive, Egyptian officers jumped in their staff cars and abandoned their men. The ensuing Six-Day War saw the coalition of Arab states lose 70,000 square kilometers of territory, despite fielding many more troops, tanks, and aircraft than their Israeli opponents.

In Armies of Sand, former CIA analyst Kenneth Pollack explores why Arab militaries have underwhelmed on the battlefield, despite routinely enjoying advantages in men and materiel. This is not simply a product of superior Israeli military sophistication. Gaddafi’s Libya suffered a series of defeats at the hands of poverty-stricken Chad, while Saddam Hussein mounted what Pollack dubs ‘one of the most pathetic military offensives of the past century’ against Iran.

There are a few common theories among experts. For example, many Arab states relied heavily on Soviet doctrine and training. This emphasized preplanned operations and centralized control. When the situation on the battlefield changed unpredictably, officers froze. During the Yom Kippur War of 1973, the Syrians broke through Israeli defenses on the Golan Heights. But instead of pressing their advantage, the Syrian troops paused, in line with their pre-war plan. In the meantime, the Israelis rushed reserves forward and retook the territory.

Another common explanation is politicization. Leaders often feared their own militaries more than those of their opponents. This led to promotions based on loyalty and purges of experienced officers. At one point, Saddam Hussein had as many as sixteen different security services, which devoted an inordinate amount of time to spying on each other.

Pollack finds these explanations lacking. Cuba and North Korea both relied on Soviet doctrine and performed creditably in their twentieth-century military engagements. After substantial depoliticization in the 1970s, Egyptian military performance remained as dismal as ever.

Instead, he argues that these failures stem from patterns common in many Arab cultures: deference to authority, loyalty to the in-group over outsiders, a premium on personal honor, and horror of shame. The fear of shame explains why Nasser’s commanders told him he was winning, while the deference to hierarchy explains why battalion officers would stick to orders long after they ceased to make sense.

Pollack locates much of this culture in formal and informal education. The Arab family is large, patriarchal, and built around the father’s unquestioned authority. Modern Arab education has its origins in the Quranic schools that were, for centuries, the main form of education in much of the region. In these schools, knowledge comes down from a higher authority, and pedagogy is based on memorization.

When governments built mass public school systems in the 1950s and 60s, they changed the syllabus but preserved the teaching methods, which emphasize rote learning over problem solving. This tendency seeps into military training, which often consists of rehearsing pre-scripted maneuvers. An American trainer working with Egypt’s elite F-16 pilots recalled that ‘they know where to turn, and where to pretend to fire munitions, and who is going to win’ before exercises started and that they would get ‘extremely upset when someone did something he was not supposed to do’.

In most Arab offices and government ministries, authority is concentrated at the top and risk taking isn’t rewarded. Bosses behave as patriarchs who lend money to staff, mediate personal disputes, and intervene in family matters. In one study of Egyptian, Saudi, and Sudanese bureaucracies, 90 percent of senior officials deemed their subordinates ‘unqualified to innovate’. The Egyptian or Iraqi lieutenant standing on the battlefield has been immersed in this worldview, likely for decades, across successive institutions.

The exceptions largely support Pollack’s case. Hezbollah emerged as a highly capable fighting force after reducing its numbers following the Lebanese Civil War. This meant they retained only the small minority of culturally atypical individuals who’d proven themselves on the battlefield. Meanwhile, Islamic State, at its 2014 peak, drew its most gifted commanders from Chechens, Uzbeks, and Tajiks.

Anyone who has interacted with a bank or government ministry in the Middle East will recognize many of the traits Pollack describes. They continue to pose a challenge for regional efforts at social and economic reform.

Alex Chalmers is a staff writer at the Cosmos Institute and a former editor at Works in Progress.

Cameron Smith has moved on from LIV Golf, is preparing for his invitation-only appearances on the DP World Tour and is already thinking about a return to the PGA Tour.

"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," Smith told the Australian Associated Press.
