How can Smith return to the PGA Tour?

Smith will not return as a full-time member on the DP World Tour, but is one of a number of former LIV players, including Dustin Johnson and Bubba Watson, to sign an agreement with the tour to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments during the 2027 season, excluding Rolex Series events.

Under the DP World Tour and PGA Tour's current agreement, the top 10 players on the Race to Dubai Rankings qualify for the PGA Tour.

However, to even have a chance at winning one of those coveted cards, Smith will need to play more tournaments on the DP World Tour's 2027 schedule.

He could do that by winning the co-sanctioned BMW Australian PGA Championship or the Australian Open at Kingston Heath, which begins on December 3 and also features Rory McIlroy.

To avoid spending their young adult lives in debt, students have long been counseled to stay in-state for college. After all, it’s the mission of public universities, funded by tax dollars, to provide an affordable, high-quality education to state residents.

Yet, in 34 states, it costs students from low-income families at least a third of their household income — upwards of $10,000 a year — to attend the state flagship university. That includes not just tuition, but also room and board and books, after accounting for all grants and scholarships — what’s known as “net price.”

Take Alabama, which had one of the highest price tags for public colleges in the country in 2024, the most recent data available. A student coming from a family in that state that earns less than $30,000 a year was expected to pay more than $19,000 annually on average for tuition and other costs at the University of Alabama, the flagship. The same went for Pennsylvania State University.

And it’s not just flagship universities. At more than half of four-year public colleges across the country, including regional public institutions as well as large research universities, in-state students from families making less than $30,000 faced this same, near-impossible financial juggling act: On average, they had to pay more than a third of their family income to attend.

Net price at public colleges has declined over the past few years, when adjusted to overall inflation, yet wages have not kept up as the costs of housing, food and health care keep rising, and low-income families continue to struggle to afford college.

Some states have done a better job of controlling costs than others. Florida — just across the state line from Alabama — had among the least expensive four-year public colleges in the country. That’s largely because the state legislature has maintained funding for higher education and capped tuition over the past decade.

Hover over the map to see the cost for each state.

Even if students from families earning less than $30,000 take out the maximum federal student loan allowed ($5,500 for first-year students), attending one of nearly 300 public four-year colleges still cost them at least $4,500 more in their first year alone, even when they stayed in-state. The same was true at more than 50 public two-year colleges that also offer bachelor’s degrees.

Hover over each dot to see the name of the college and the average cost.

The situation wasn’t much better for students from families making between $30,000 and $48,000. They needed to come up with a sizable share of their annual income, $5,000 — after all scholarships and maximum student loans — at close to 300 four-year public colleges, even when they enrolled in-state.

About 1 in 6 American households earns less than $30,000 a year. More than 1 in 4 earn less than $50,000.

State flagship universities boast some of the highest graduation and job placement rates among public universities, which makes them a crucial path to a secure financial future for students who grew up in poverty. Their affordability, however, depends on where you live.

Students from families who make less than $30,000 paid just over $1,000 out of pocket for tuition and other costs at the University of Michigan and roughly $2,000 at the state flagships in Florida, North Carolina and Illinois. Pennsylvania State University and the University of Alabama were the most expensive for low-income families, but the state flagships in New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon and Iowa all also cost students whose families make less than $30,000 more than half their annual income.

It’s not just the flagship that’s pricey in Alabama. The state’s other public colleges were among the most expensive in the country on average for families who make less than $48,000. (A spokesman from the University of Alabama said that the average net price for families making less than $30,000 dropped by about 6 percent in 2024-25, which brought it to about $18,000; it decreased by 12 percent for families making between $30,001 and $48,000, he said.)

The University of North Alabama, which cost low-income students the least in the state, still had a net price of close to $10,000. And half of Alabama’s public colleges cost more than $14,000 for students whose families make less than $30,000.

There are less expensive public colleges scattered around the country, and some students save money by starting at a community college and then transferring, although that path isn’t always available. At just over 60 public four-year colleges, the net price for families who make less than $30,000 was $5,000 or less in 2024. New York City, where most students don’t live on campus, hosts seven colleges that cost less than $1,600.

Methodology:

Where does this data come from? These charts use the federal government’s definition of net price, which is an attempt to capture the total cost of attendance for a student. It includes room and board, books and supplies, tuition and required fees, minus any grants and scholarships for first-time, full-time, dependent students (those who are still under the care of their parents). Median household income nationally was about $81,600 in 2024, but it varies widely by state, from a high of close to $105,000 in Massachusetts to about $59,000 in Mississippi.

item.title: What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

Where Rates Come From

The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate, which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful for educators

Lexile Level Alternatives

Reading assessment tools measure different things: how accurately a student reads, what the student understands, or how difficult a text is likely to be.

A student who reads a passage accurately may still misunderstand it. Research distinguishes word recognition from the language and knowledge needed for comprehension (Castles et al., 2018). Choose an assessment by the question it needs to answer.

Which tool fits the task?

Tools for assessing students

1. DIBELS 8th Edition

DIBELS uses short assessments to identify students who may need reading support and measure progress. Its oral reading fluency assessment, used in grades 1–8, requires a student to read a supplied passage aloud for one minute while the teacher marks errors on a separate copy.

Skipped or incorrectly read words count as errors. If a student hesitates for three seconds, the examiner supplies the word and marks it incorrect. A word self-corrected within three seconds counts as correct. The teacher calculates words correct per minute and reading accuracy, then checks the benchmark for the student’s grade and testing period.

The oral reading scores do not directly test understanding of the passage. Fuchs et al. (2001) reviewed evidence supporting oral reading fluency as an indicator of broader reading competence. That research supports the assessment approach; it does not, by itself, validate the current DIBELS edition.

Access: Download student passages, scoring forms, benchmarks, and administration instructions from the University of Oregon’s DIBELS materials page at no cost. Follow the administration guide and do not rehearse assessment passages with students.

2. easyCBM

easyCBM provides reading assessments and graphs showing a student’s scores across testing dates. Tasks include reading words or passages aloud and answering multiple-choice comprehension questions. Available measures depend on grade and account type.

A teacher can administer different passage-reading forms at successive checks and enter the scores to track words correct per minute. Use designated progress-monitoring forms at the same assessment level; changing passage difficulty makes the scores harder to compare.

Access: Create an account through easyCBM’s Teacher Edition. The free Lite tier includes progress-monitoring assessments, individual graphs, and item-level reports. Benchmark assessments and benchmark risk reports require a paid edition. The edition comparison lists which measures each account includes.

3. Qualitative Reading Inventory, Seventh Edition (QRI-7)

QRI-7 is an individually administered assessment with graded word lists and narrative and informational passages from pre-primer through high school. Teachers record oral reading errors and assess understanding through retelling and questions about the passage.

Teachers use the inventory’s criteria to estimate independent, instructional, and frustration levels for the passages assessed. These results describe performance on those tasks; they are not interchangeable with a Lexile measure.

Access: Purchase QRI-7 from Pearson or use a school-owned copy. The manual includes administration, scoring, and technical-development information. Administration requires time for one-to-one reading, comprehension questions, and scoring.

4. Star Reading

Star Reading is a computer-adaptive assessment: question difficulty changes in response to the student’s answers. Students answer questions on a device; Renaissance reports a typical testing time of about 20 minutes.

Reports include a scaled score for tracking performance and a percentile rank for comparison with students in the same grade. Schools use these results to screen students and monitor achievement.

Because Star Reading does not assess oral reading, its results do not show which words a student mispronounces or how the student reads aloud.

Access: Students and teachers sign in through their school’s Renaissance subscription. Star Reading and Star Early Literacy are separate assessments; verify which one the school provides.

Tools for checking text difficulty

5. Lexile Find a Book and Text Analyzer

Find a Book lets teachers look up a book or search by Lexile measure and interest. Use it to identify possible texts when a student already has a Lexile measure from an assessment. Searching by the student’s enrolled grade does not establish that student’s reading ability.

The classroom Text Analyzer accepts prose passages of up to 500 words and returns a 200L-wide range, rather than a single certified measure. It is not designed to produce valid measures for poetry, song lyrics, recipes, or lists.

Access: Both tools are available through the Lexile & Quantile Hub. Find a Book offers limited searches without registration and unlimited searches with a free Basic+ account. Text Analyzer requires Premium access; eligible educators in partner states receive it at no cost after registering with their school or district email address.

6. Microsoft Word readability statistics

Word reports Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level, calculated from average sentence length and syllables per word. Teachers can use these statistics to check assignment directions or compare drafts of a passage.

Access: In Word for Microsoft 365 on the Current Channel, select Home → Editor → Document stats. Other supported versions use proofing settings. Microsoft’s readability instructions give the steps by version. The feature is included with supported Word software; it does not assess a student.

Use the result to choose the next check

If a student reads slowly or makes frequent errors, examine word reading more closely. If the student reads accurately but cannot explain the passage, assess comprehension rather than assigning a lower level from speed alone. Record the tool, date, passage or test level, and score so later results can be compared meaningfully.…

item.title: The Game Is the Easy Part: Measuring Military Strategic Judgment
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Thought-provoking topic with a focus on strategic judgment and AI

go beyond the headlines.

Thomas Nagle

November 24, 2026

If a colonel and a Navy captain made the same decisions for the same reasons in a graded wargame, would they get the same score?

This question stopped being an academic thought experiment on Nov. 9, 2026. Speaking at the Naval War College, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that “competitive [AI] assisted wargaming and high-stress decision forcing scenarios” would become the “centerpiece of senior officer evaluation.” Further, “these exercises [would] feed directly” into the newly established joint warfighter evaluations: the new assessments for colonels and captains competing for their first star. A memorandum issued the same day directs every staff and war college to establish a “rigorous, standardized culminating capstone wargame or comprehensive exam … to support talent management and stratification decisions.” Despite historical precedents, that is a great deal to ask of a wargame, which is no longer restricted to exploring a problem or teaching a lesson, but will be used to rank people. This is a departure from how they are typically used today in the department.

A test with such high stakes should meet three standards. First, it measures what matters for leaders at this level, rather than how well-suited an officer’s experience happens to be for a specific scenario. Second, it gives the same grade for the same performance, no matter who grades it or how many times. Third, because these officers will compete for joint positions, a grade earned in one service’s evaluation should mean the same thing as another’s.

In other words, the wargaming tests should be valid, repeatable, and comparable. The wargaming field itself has long held that its games produce insight, not measurement, and there is little published evidence that a wargame can meet these criteria despite decades of experience. The memo from the secretary directed a framework to accomplish this in 180 days.

The required scale and frequency to reach proficiency at the format and content in varying contexts make this harder. Officers will be graded on judgment in these games, which can only be built through repeated practice with feedback over years. Expanding the use of AI assessments is a requirement to make this work, but a machine’s feedback is only useful if it can be trusted.

I believe it can be done, and I have spent the past year working on this problem set. I write this as the founder of WarPaths, a platform that grades and assesses individual wargame play. As such, I have an interest in defense contracting for AI usage in the classroom. The first AI-enabled grader I built failed multiple tests I assumed it would pass. I found that the game itself is the easy part and the details of the assessment are the hard part. Delivering the valid, repeatable, and comparable wargaming tests at the necessary scale creates a unique set of challenges.

The memorandum’s specified tasks are straightforward. The military departments should build the capstone and deliver a “standardized assessment and grading framework within 180 days.” Most of the officers’ grades are to come from “objective evaluations such as wargames, planning exercises, strategic essays, and decision-forcing cases.” Critically, the first directive in the memorandum requires that institutional program learning objectives focus on “comprehensive understanding across all domains of warfare.” Service-centric games and evaluation approaches will not suffice.

The memorandum’s implied tasks for wargaming are much more difficult. First, deciding what to measure is the necessary starting point. How much of the grade or assessment is attached to game outcomes versus the reasoning behind the decisions? How is the right balance achieved between strategic reasoning and operational effectiveness? Both play a role in the secretary’s speech and memo.

Second, stakeholders should demonstrate that grading of the tests consistently produces enough distribution to reliably stratify participants — one of the secretary’s requirements — into performance bands. Without this consistent stratification, the intended outcomes of the memo cannot be achieved: Boards would not be able to reliably distinguish good performances from outstanding ones.

Third, this should work at the required scale and frequency. Scale is the number of officers assessed individually. Frequency is how often each should practice, with feedback, to build the judgment being tested. Both are beyond what instructors can do by hand.

The wargaming community largely holds that games as they are typically utilized in the Department of Defense resist quantification. The chair of the Naval War College’s War Gaming Department and two colleagues argued on this site just last year that asking wargames for quantitative precision misunderstands the method. A further complicating factor is the nature of how games are normally built, which is well set in practice. Designed to facilitate discussion, games are built around specific learning objectives with the participants in mind.

So, the wargaming field’s product is typically collective, bespoke, qualitative, and used to learn. The directives require a product that is individual, standardized, objective, comparable across institutions, and used to rank.

The field is correct in that a game cannot measure the war. The question the secretary’s memo raises is: Can a game measure the warfighter, and if so, what are the requirements?…

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

'Very poor' letters

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme, the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system.

Benefits review to suggest quicker payment for some disabled people

A review into the main disability benefit is set to recommend that those with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses should get quicker payments.

The report on Personal Independence Payment (Pip) will also suggest overhauling assessments so they provide claimants in England and Wales with more appropriate support.

But it is understood not to suggest major savings, despite the benefit's cost being projected to more than double between 2020 and 2030.

Groups representing disabled people - who had a hand in drafting the report - have broadly welcomed its findings.

About four million people claim Pip, which is set to cost about Â£32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to Â£41.5bn in 2030-31. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost Â£16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

Chaired by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, the review was set up last year after the Starmer government's aborted attempt to cut welfare spending.

Sir Stephen has proposed linking disability benefit payments to real-life needs and that extra costs be incurred by the claimant.

Those with the most severe and persistent conditions would be fast-tracked with no further assessments involved - believed to be the case for about one in 10 claimants - with the aim of creating a "less burdensome" process, Sir Stephen wrote in The Times.

There were concerns from disability charities that Pip payments might become means-tested or the cash payments partially replaced with vouchers, but it is understood this will not be the case.

Frankie Bowyer from Scope UK told the BBC that disabled people found the assessment process "stressful and degrading".

"People have described to us feeling that assessors were trying to catch them out, trying to minimise their needs and that's really not want we want to see," Bowyer said.

Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about Â£500 every four weeks.

The mum-of-two, a trained benefits adviser, told the BBC that even she found the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing".

"Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust.

"Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."

Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university. She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further Â£1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages.

"The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house," she said.

Matt Ryder from the Adam Smith Institute, a free-market think tank said disability claims had risen fastest amongst young people "who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic".

"We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that," he said.

"It's where the cost is heading... According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to Â£47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?"

Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.

It suggested removing Pip from this group would save up to Â£4.4m a year.

Lindsay Judge from the Resolution Foundation said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, this "should be possible nonetheless" and that "major change is needed".

She said improvements should include assessments that "better understand disabled people's needs" as well as awards in the form of cash or services that "better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face" as well as "more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood".

The review's proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

Why it is here: Political analysis with implications for EU relations

Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?

When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader, promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

- My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published â the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed â and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas â Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

item.title: The Never-Ending China-US Story
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Historical perspective on China-US relations

On November 19, U.S. President Donald Trump met China’s President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It was the latest in a sequence of encounters and agreements that Washington has repeatedly presented as signs of renewed stability in the relationship. It was, in other words, another “breakthrough” – except that it was not quite clear what had been broken through, since the principal economic, technological, and strategic disputes between Washington and Beijing remained unresolved.

To be clear, that is not necessarily a criticism of the meeting. Diplomacy does not have to produce a grand settlement to be useful. But there is something revealing about the language surrounding China-U.S. relations. Again and again, Washington narrates the relationship as though the latest development might provide a decisive turning point. Then the same old story starts again.

This has been particularly visible during Trump’s second administration. In May, after Trump’s visit to Beijing, the White House announced that the United States and China had reached a “historic” agreement intended to “enhance stability and confidence for businesses and consumers around the world.” The two sides also agreed to “build a constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity.”

In September, Xi traveled to Washington for a state visit. Trump described their relationship as “a friendship – a truly great friendship, actually – built on mutual respect.” At the state dinner, he said that the two countries could continue building a relationship that promoted prosperity and security for future generations.

The White House subsequently described the visit as advancing a “fair and reciprocal relationship” and “operationalizing” the trade and investment mechanisms established during the May summit. Again, Xi’s visit was deemed to be “historic.”

Trump himself was even more expansive. At the state dinner, he said that the two countries had “never gotten along better” and that they could together “build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations.”

Two months later, Trump was back in China. In comments to the press, Trump emphasized the supposedly singular nature of his reception in China: “the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people… the soldiers, the whole thing. It was a great respect, and I appreciate that.”

From Beijing to Washington to Shenzhen, each meeting produced the language of progress and was presented as a new stage in the relationship.

And yet, between these “historic” diplomatic moments, the underlying disputes didn’t disappear. On November 6 – less than two weeks before the Shenzhen meeting – U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was still pressing Beijing “to fully implement its past commitments” to buy U.S. agricultural goods and ease export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals.

There is a tendency, especially on Washington’s part, to talk about the China-U.S. relationship as though each new development is bringing it closer to an imaginary ending. Each time, it turns out to be just another chapter of the same story.

The pattern can be seen not only in the on-again, off-again nature of summit diplomacy, but also in the recurring sequence of tariffs and tariff suspensions, export controls and negotiations over technology, and disputes over rare earths and agricultural purchases. Each time a new agreement is reached, it supposedly resets the relationship, only for the pattern to repeat itself.

Biden’s China Story

This pattern is not unique to Trump, however. Former President Joe Biden’s approach also depended on a narrative about how the China-U.S. relationship could be stabilized and managed.

Biden told a very different story about China. His administration generally avoided the language of dramatic personal deals and instead emphasized responsible competition and “guardrails” against conflict.

At the November 2023 summit in Woodside, California, Biden described the task in remarkably different terms than Trump would later use. Competition between the United States and China was unavoidable – indeed, it was already underway, Biden argued. However, it had to be managed “responsibly to prevent it from veering into conflict, confrontation, or a new Cold War.” Biden and Xi agreed to maintain communication and work to prevent the China-U.S. rivalry from sparking a wider crisis.

Biden’s approach was therefore less about finding a decisive deal than about establishing a stable framework for managing competition. That was a different political genre, but it still supplied a narrative about how political action could give direction to an uncertain relationship, implicitly supplanting the old way of dealing with China.

But for all their differences, there is an important similarity in Biden’s and Trump’s China policies: both approaches hinge on a story about where the relationship is going. Both reduce a sprawling and continuing relationship into a sequence of moments. And both center on the idea that the president’s leadership is breaking new ground in the relationship. And both depend, to some degree, on the idea that political action can give history a discernible direction.

Tragicomic Emplotment

This is where the concept of “tragicomic emplotment” becomes useful. In my research on China-U.S. relations, I use the term to describe a narrative form in which grave stakes coexist with repeated expectations that recovery, restoration, or victory remain possible through resolve and leadership.

The term does not mean that China-U.S. relations are funny. The stakes are genuinely tragic, particularly the possibility that competition between two nuclear-armed powers could lead to conflict. The comic element, instead, is the repeated expectation of closure.…

Why it is here: Environmental issue with cross-border implications

Thailand is set to ban the export and transit of chemicals used in rare-earth mining ‌amid mounting concerns over the pollution of Thai rivers by mining operations in Myanmar, the country’s deputy prime minister said on Saturday.

Speaking to the media after a meeting of the National Disaster Prevention and Mitigation Command in Bangkok, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said that the government was committed to “leveraging every possible avenue” to address cross-border pollution, including by cracking down on the illegal export of hazardous chemicals.

He also announced six measures to protect communities in Thailand from cross-border contamination. Among these was a tightening of controls on mineral imports and exports through Thailand from Myanmar, in order to “close legal loopholes and prevent Thailand from being used as a channel for the unregulated mining activities in Myanmar,” Thai PBS reported.

He said that the government also plans to set up an advanced testing lab to monitor water quality, supply clean water to affected residents, and establish an agri-mapping system that will designate areas of the country as red, yellow, or green in accordance with the prevailing levels of toxicity. Yodchanan added that a 150-kilometer stretch of the Kok River, a tributary of the Mekong River in northern Thailand, would be designated a pollution control zone from December 2.

Since early 2025, Thai authorities have detected rising levels of arsenic, heavy metals, and other toxic compounds in rivers in northern Thailand. The Kok, Sai, and Ruak rivers, all tributaries of the Mekong, have recorded elevated arsenic and heavy metal levels tied to gold and rare-earth mining operations in Myanmar’s Shan State. These chemicals have also been detected in the Mekong River itself, as well as in the Salween and Kraburi rivers, both of which form portions of the border between Myanmar and Thailand.

This issue, like many other toxic recent trends in Myanmar’s political economy, can be linked to the military coup of 2021 and the subsequent inflammation of the country’s civil war. As Mongabay has reported, “The detection of heavy metals coincided with a rapid expansion of unregulated mining of gold, rare earth elements, and other critical minerals across Myanmar, largely driven by a collapsing post-coup economy, ongoing conflict, and rapidly rising global demand for critical minerals.”

Yodchanan also said that Thailand had contacted the governments of China and Myanmar about the contamination issue, and that Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuanketkaew will join ministerial-level discussions with representatives from both countries tomorrow. This will be followed by further working-level discussions involving Thailand’s permanent secretary for natural resources and environment that hope to “identify and address upstream pollution sources.” Sihasak also reportedly discussed the issue with Myanmar’s military-backed leader Min Aung Hlaing during a trip to Naypyidaw earlier this month; it was also discussed during Min Aung Hlaing’s state visit to Thailand in August.

Whether bilateral diplomacy can successfully address the issue remains to be seen. In August, Myanmar and Thailand signed an agreement on the establishment of a cooperative mechanism to monitor and track water quality and share data related to water quality in border and transboundary rivers. Leaving aside the lack of action on this front – the agreement has been harshly criticized by civil society groups for being diluted at Myanmar’s request – Mongabay reported on November 17 that the joint working group born out of the agreement has not met even once since it was signed.

Perhaps a bigger challenge is that most of the relevant mining operations, like the scourge of online scamming operations that have attracted so much attention in recent years, lie in territories controlled by armed rebel groups such as the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and United Wa State Army (UWSA).

A recent analysis by Mongabay, which has done in-depth reporting on the river pollution issue, showed that of the 2,245 mining sites identified by the U.S.-based Stimson Center, just 577 are located in areas under central government control. While Thailand and China have long had informal relations with groups like the UWSA and KIA, Myanmar’s government opposes any official recognition of or outreach to these groups.

As with many issues in Myanmar, the determination to view the central government as the sole locus of diplomatic legitimacy complicates any attempt to address directly the problem of unregulated mining operations in Myanmar. Barring such direct engagement with Myanmar’s various rebel groups, the Thai government is only going to be able to tackle the issue through indirect and attenuated means.
